articles.body:
## Scope

A reported zero resistance means that a specified measurement cannot resolve a resistive voltage under its current, geometry and acquisition conditions. It is evidence within a detection limit, not a measurement of a mathematically exact zero. Keep the measured signal, correction and uncertainty together; a display reading of zero does not specify all three. The uncertainty framework below is separate from a microscopic theory of superconductivity. [R6](#ref-source-0c63f38b6789c792)

Record transition onset, midpoint and the operational zero criterion separately. A conducting path need not occupy the whole specimen. As a simple counterexample, two ideal parallel channels have $R_{\mathrm{eff}}=R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2)$: one zero-resistance channel shorts a finite-resistance channel. This circuit result establishes no volume fraction or material identity. Magnetic and thermodynamic probes answer complementary questions.

## Mathematical assumptions

Suppose a corrected voltage estimate is $\hat V$ and the applied current estimate is $\hat I$. If independently justified intervals satisfy $|V-\hat V|\le U_V$ and $|I-\hat I|\le U_I<|\hat I|$, the triangle inequality gives a conditional bound:

$$\left|\frac{V}{I}\right|\le\frac{|\hat V|+U_V}{|\hat I|-U_I}.$$

This is a local interval calculation, not an automatically calibrated confidence statement. If the input intervals have probabilistic coverage, the output statement must retain that coverage model and their dependence. An operational threshold $|\hat V|<V_{\mathrm{cut}}$ alone does not establish $|V|<V_{\mathrm{cut}}$. Do not substitute a display digit or a noise standard deviation for a validated bound without explaining the choice. NIST's uncertainty guidance distinguishes uncertainty components, applied corrections and coverage. [R6](#ref-source-0c63f38b6789c792)

For a fixed linear resistance and equal opposite currents, model the readings as $V_+=IR+V_{0,+}+\epsilon_+$ and $V_-=-IR+V_{0,-}+\epsilon_-$. Then

$$\hat R=\frac{V_+-V_-}{2I}=R+\frac{V_{0,+}-V_{0,-}+\epsilon_+-\epsilon_-}{2I}.$$

A constant current-even offset cancels. Drift, a current-odd voltage, unequal currents or a changing specimen do not satisfy that cancellation. NIST's shunt report describes a thermoelectric contribution that reverses with the current and therefore survives ordinary reversal averaging. Its apparatus-specific thermal treatment is not a universal correction for superconducting samples. [R5](#ref-source-c8143afdf96ce96f)

With fixed known $I$, the voltage contribution to standard uncertainty is $u_R^2=[u_+^2+u_-^2-2\operatorname{cov}(V_+,V_-)]/(4I^2)$. Current uncertainty and model/systematic contributions must be included separately when present. Independent algebra and finite-outcome checks verify this conditional variance and show why assuming uncorrelated errors can fail. The check is not an instrument calibration. [R6](#ref-source-0c63f38b6789c792)

Converting resistance to resistivity as $\rho=RA/L$ additionally assumes the appropriate homogeneous current path, area $A$ and voltage-contact separation $L$. Four-terminal geometry does not by itself establish uniform current density. Conversely, a passive lumped loop with constant inductance $L_{\mathrm{loop}}$ and resistance obeys $I(t)=I_0e^{-Rt/L_{\mathrm{loop}}}$. A measured fractional decay no larger than $\varepsilon$ gives $R\le-L_{\mathrm{loop}}\ln(1-\varepsilon)/t$ only under that loop model. Vortex relaxation or changing inductance needs a different treatment.

## Experimental criteria

Halperin and Nelson's 1979 superconducting-film theory describes a vortex-unbinding regime, fluctuation conductivity and nonlinear resistivity. This supports a limited theoretical reference for thin-film analysis, not a universal fit or a pairing-symmetry test. The publisher abstract was checked; its full derivation has not yet been reviewed here. [R2](#ref-source-9e55a4505d9de546)

Use four-terminal measurements where the time scale and apparatus permit them, and state the actual geometry when they do not. Publish the voltage/current data, detection criterion, field orientation, temperature sweep, bandwidth or integration time and contact configuration. Check current dependence, contact stability and thermal response. Treat these as editorial evidence requirements rather than a claim that one fixed protocol fits every apparatus.

If contacts or backgrounds are subtracted, preserve the original reading and propagate the uncertainty of the subtraction. An independent magnetic or heat-capacity result on a comparable sample helps test a bulk interpretation. A low transport reading alone cannot exclude a connected minority phase, a short or an instrument limitation.

## Limits and disputes

Mitrano and colleagues' earlier author manuscript reports transient optical signatures in driven K3C60 and discusses a high-mobility alternative interpretation. Such spectra do not constitute a direct DC transport measurement. This check covers selected 2015 manuscript passages; the publisher record flags an update whose details have not been verified here. No optical crossover temperature is entered as an equilibrium transition. [R3](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1)

Budden and colleagues complement optics with a 1 ns electrical probe of a driven K3C60 pellet at 100 K. The checked manuscript uses a two-terminal transient measurement with contact resistance calibrated against static four-terminal measurements. Figure 4 explicitly includes a calibration-related systematic uncertainty. A resistance compatible with zero in this driven experiment is not an equilibrium $T_{c,\mathrm{zero}}$. The numerical waveform and complete final journal version were not independently reanalyzed. [R4](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690)

These methods probe different observables and time windows. Keep optical extrapolation to zero frequency separate from electrical response, and distinguish either from long-time equilibrium transport. A very large photoconductivity can motivate further tests without resolving every question about phase coherence or magnetic expulsion.

## Discovery implications

A useful discovery report states which observations would distinguish a superconducting path from a contact artifact, minority phase or alternative conducting state. Repeat under controlled current and magnetic field, retain unsuccessful controls, and seek independent probes of the claimed phase. Field suppression supports an interpretation but does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction.

BCS theory is retained as a microscopic background reference, with its detailed treatment in the linked BCS entry. It is not the source for the measurement bounds or procedural requirements developed here. Keep operational transport evidence, theoretical interpretation and claims of bulk superconductivity distinct. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Related topics

Read [Meissner evidence](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [specific heat](/scwiki/specific-heat-jump), [critical current](/scwiki/critical-current), [BCS theory](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), [two-dimensional superconductivity](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces), and [Planckian dissipation](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation).

NIST's shunt report describes a thermoelectric contribution that reverses with the current and therefore survives ordinary reversal averaging. Its apparatus-specific thermal treatment is not a universal correction for superconducting samples. [R5](#ref-source-c8143afdf96ce96f)

With fixed known $I$, the voltage contribution to standard uncertainty is $u_R^2=[u_+^2+u_-^2-2\operatorname{cov}(V_+,V_-)]/(4I^2)$. Current uncertainty and model/systematic contributions must be included separately when present. Independent algebra and finite-outcome checks verify this conditional variance and show why assuming uncorrelated errors can fail. The check is not an instrument calibration. [R6](#ref-source-0c63f38b6789c792)

Converting resistance to resistivity as $\rho=RA/L$ additionally assumes the appropriate homogeneous current path, area $A$ and voltage-contact separation $L$. Four-terminal geometry does not by itself establish uniform current density. Conversely, a passive lumped loop with constant inductance $L_{\mathrm{loop}}$ and resistance obeys $I(t)=I_0e^{-Rt/L_{\mathrm{loop}}}$. A measured fractional decay no larger than $\varepsilon$ gives $R\le-L_{\mathrm{loop}}\ln(1-\varepsilon)/t$ only under that loop model. Vortex relaxation or changing inductance needs a different treatment.

## Experimental criteria

Halperin and Nelson's 1979 superconducting-film theory describes a vortex-unbinding regime, fluctuation conductivity and nonlinear resistivity. This supports a limited theoretical reference for thin-film analysis, not a universal fit or a pairing-symmetry test. The publisher abstract was checked; its full derivation has not yet been reviewed here. [R2](#ref-source-9e55a4505d9de546)

Use four-terminal measurements where the time scale and apparatus permit them, and state the actual geometry when they do not. Publish the voltage/current data, detection criterion, field orientation, temperature sweep, bandwidth or integration time and contact configuration. Check current dependence, contact stability and thermal response. Treat these as editorial evidence requirements rather than a claim that one fixed protocol fits every apparatus.

If contacts or backgrounds are subtracted, preserve the original reading and propagate the uncertainty of the subtraction. An independent magnetic or heat-capacity result on a comparable sample helps test a bulk interpretation. A low transport reading alone cannot exclude a connected minority phase, a short or an instrument limitation.

## Limits and disputes

Mitrano and colleagues' earlier author manuscript reports transient optical signatures in driven K3C60 and discusses a high-mobility alternative interpretation. Such spectra do not constitute a direct DC transport measurement. This check covers selected 2015 manuscript passages; the publisher record flags an update whose details have not been verified here. No optical crossover temperature is entered as an equilibrium transition. [R3](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1)

Budden and colleagues complement optics with a 1 ns electrical probe of a driven K3C60 pellet at 100 K. The checked manuscript uses a two-terminal transient measurement with contact resistance calibrated against static four-terminal measurements. Figure 4 explicitly includes a calibration-related systematic uncertainty. A resistance compatible with zero in this driven experiment is not an equilibrium $T_{c,\mathrm{zero}}$. The numerical waveform and complete final journal version were not independently reanalyzed. [R4](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690)

These methods probe different observables and time windows. Keep optical extrapolation to zero frequency separate from electrical response, and distinguish either from long-time equilibrium transport. A very large photoconductivity can motivate further tests without resolving every question about phase coherence or magnetic expulsion.

## Discovery implications

A useful discovery report states which observations would distinguish a superconducting path from a contact artifact, minority phase or alternative conducting state. Repeat under controlled current and magnetic field, retain unsuccessful controls, and seek independent probes of the claimed phase. Field suppression supports an interpretation but does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction.

BCS theory is retained as a microscopic background reference, with its detailed treatment in the linked BCS entry. It is not the source for the measurement bounds or procedural requirements developed here. Keep operational transport evidence, theoretical interpretation and claims of bulk superconductivity distinct. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

articles.body:
## Scope

Quasiparticle interference (QPI) uses spatial variations in scanning tunneling conductance to constrain electronic states and scattering. Elastic scattering can connect states of equal energy with momentum transfer $\mathbf q=\mathbf k'-\mathbf k$. A Fourier peak is a feature of a measured response, not a direct photograph of a Fermi surface or a uniquely identified order parameter. Keep the tunneling matrix element, defect channel and preprocessing attached to every interpretation.

In a weak-tunneling description with a sufficiently smooth tip spectrum and matrix element, low-temperature differential conductance can approximate a sample's local density of states. Thermal and instrumental convolution, spatially varying set points and orbital sensitivity can change that relation. A conductance map and an ideal local-density-of-states calculation should not be treated as interchangeable without testing these assumptions.

## Mathematical assumptions

With the convention $\tilde g(\mathbf q,E)=\sum_{\mathbf r}e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}g(\mathbf r,E)$, a translated pattern obeys

$$g'(\mathbf r,E)=g(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0,E),\qquad\tilde g'=e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r_0}\tilde g.$$

Its Fourier magnitude is unchanged, while its real and imaginary parts generally change. A real map satisfies $\tilde g(-\mathbf q)=\tilde g(\mathbf q)^*$. Independent discrete-transform checks verify both identities, an exactly sampled cosine and sampling aliases. Finite cropping can also change amplitudes; the exact translation identity assumes the whole pattern or periodic data, not two differently cropped fields.

For a periodic lattice with $N$ sites and one defect at the origin, define an ideal electron-block response

$$\Lambda(\mathbf q,E)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf k}[G_0(\mathbf k,E)\,T(E)\,G_0(\mathbf k-\mathbf q,E)]_{11}.$$

Here $G_0$ is a retarded Nambu Green function and $T=[1-Vg_0]^{-1}V$, with $g_0=N^{-1}\sum_{\mathbf k}G_0$. The Fourier transform of the spin-resolved electron density-of-states change is

$$\delta\tilde\rho(\mathbf q,E)=-\frac{\Lambda(\mathbf q,E)-\Lambda(-\mathbf q,E)^*}{2\pi i}.$$

Taking just $-\operatorname{Im}\Lambda(\mathbf q)/\pi$ is insufficient for a general complex Fourier map. It becomes valid with the additional even-in-momentum response condition. Six independent checks compare full real-space resolvent inversion with the scattering expression on a ten-site, fixed-gap model; displaced defects expose the lost phase. This is a normalization and response check, not a cuprate or FeSe simulation. The selected Wang–Lee manuscript supplies the broader scattering framework and explicitly discusses off-shell and matrix-element limits. [R2](#ref-source-6e0b3a25ead07f3c)

A joint-density-of-states construction counts candidate equal-energy connections but omits scattering amplitudes and coherence factors. In an ideal equal-magnitude, real-gap Fermi-surface limit, scalar and magnetic Born amplitudes contain $uu'-vv'$ and $uu'+vv'$. Setting $u=u'=1/\sqrt2$ and $v=\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta)/\sqrt2$ interchanges their zero/nonzero weights when the relative gap sign changes. This conditional example explains sensitivity to the impurity channel; it does not identify a real defect from one bright peak. [R2](#ref-source-6e0b3a25ead07f3c)

## Experimental criteria

Hoffman and colleagues' dispersing-QPI manuscript reports Bi2212 conductance imaging at 4.2 K. Selected pages describe two peak families with opposite energy trends and doping-dependent dispersion, interpreted against photoemission information. Its Science DOI ends in **1072640**. The inherited DOI ending in **1066974** instead identifies their distinct vortex-core modulation paper; these are not interchangeable evidence. [R1](#ref-source-e8e6ef56da103435) [R5](#ref-source-353efd52d3443260)

Sprau and colleagues' FeSe manuscript reports imaging at 280 mK. The relative-sign analysis uses the real parts at opposite energies, isolates an interband momentum region and places the Fourier origin at a defect. Selected supplementary passages vary the integration area and repeat the analysis on additional impurities. The reported sign inference is conditional on their scattering model and band assignment; it is not an inference from the absolute Fourier intensity alone. [R4](#ref-source-2f227038c5cf73a9)

Report field of view, pixel spacing, spatial drift correction, bias grid, temperature, excitation amplitude, tip condition, set-point protocol and defect selection. Preserve both raw and processed maps. State whether a displayed quantity is a complex transform, its real part, magnitude, power or a ratio: these operations retain different information. Explain normalization, windowing, background removal, symmetrization and peak uncertainties.

## Limits and disputes

For $N_x$ equally spaced pixels of spacing $a_x$, the periodic-transform length is $L_x=N_xa_x$ and angular-wavevector bin spacing is $2\pi/L_x$; the Nyquist bound is $\pi/a_x$. Using cycles per length removes the $2\pi$ factors. Zero padding interpolates the transform but does not create a larger measured field. A window trades spectral leakage against peak width, so bin spacing alone is not an experimental uncertainty or guaranteed resolving power.

Energy dispersion supports a scattering interpretation only together with band, defect and temperature/field controls. Weak dispersion over a limited window does not by itself prove charge order; Bragg, structural, moire and electronic features can overlap. Conversely, an order and QPI may coexist. The cuprate octet geometry must not be imposed on arbitrary multiband spectra.

The McElroy reference in the pinned chapter used an unrelated biology DOI, **nature02269**. The correct QPI paper is **nature01496**; its publisher identity is checked here, while its detailed data remain outside this entry's review. The original source is preserved and the replacement recorded. [R3](#ref-source-230ea3ac9496dc90)

## Discovery implications

Use QPI to compare explicit candidate electronic and scattering models against multiple observables. A useful claim states which alternatives the data discriminate, which are still compatible, and how uncertainty in defect identity or preprocessing changes the result. Combine gap-magnitude constraints with independent bulk and phase-sensitive evidence before assigning a pairing state or mechanism.

## Related topics

Continue with [superconducting gaps](/scwiki/superconducting-gap), [Andreev reflection](/scwiki/andreev-reflection), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), [iron-based superconductors](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus).

articles.body:
## Scope

The Meissner effect describes magnetic flux exclusion from superconducting material in the appropriate equilibrium, low-field state. It adds information beyond persistent current or zero resistance. The London brothers explicitly distinguished their magnetic-state condition from an acceleration-only description that can retain the initial field. Their historical equations are used here in a modern SI convention, within a stated local model. [R2](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

The 1933 Meissner–Ochsenfeld report compares the external field around tin and lead before and after cooling through the transition. It also describes field retained in the cavity of a hollow lead tube. A field in that cavity is not a measurement of field penetrating the superconducting wall. Selected pages of a reproduction containing the original German and an English translation were checked; the historical experiment was not independently reproduced. [R1](#ref-source-512705f3e64d88d7)

Separate zero-field-cooled shielding, field-cooled magnetization and hysteresis. A type-II specimen can contain vortices, and pinning can prevent equilibration during cooling or field sweeps. Thus a protocol-dependent signal should not be labeled complete equilibrium flux expulsion. The vortex review supplies qualitative context; it is not a calibration of a particular sample's volume fraction. [R6](#ref-source-82f53ca35625217d)

## Mathematical assumptions

In a homogeneous, isotropic, vortex-free local London model, with displacement current neglected, combine the magnetic London relation with Ampere's law and $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$:

$$\nabla\times\mathbf j=-\frac{\mathbf B}{\mu_0\lambda^2},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf j,\qquad \nabla^2\mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf B}{\lambda^2}.$$

For a half-space $x>0$ with parallel surface field $B(0)=B_0$ and bounded field at depth, the solution is $B(x)=B_0e^{-x/\lambda}$. The surface boundary and exclusion of a growing solution matter; the differential equation alone does not specify an arbitrary specimen's field map. These are modern local-model deductions, not a claim that London theory covers every superconducting state. [R2](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

For an infinite slab $-a<x<a$ with equal parallel fields on its two faces, no vortices and constant $\lambda$, the same boundary-value problem gives

$$\frac{B(x)}{B_0}=\frac{\cosh(x/\lambda)}{\cosh(a/\lambda)},\qquad \chi_{\parallel}=\frac{\langle B\rangle}{B_0}-1=\frac{\lambda}{a}\tanh\!\left(\frac{a}{\lambda}\right)-1.$$

Here $2a$ is the full thickness and $B_0=\mu_0H_a$. A local finite-difference solution independently checks the field profile and its spatial average. A thick slab tends toward $\chi_{\parallel}=-1$; a very thin slab in this parallel geometry has much weaker shielding even when the entire slab obeys the superconducting model. This is not a formula for a perpendicular-field thin film or a porous specimen.

Demagnetization is a separate shape effect. For an ellipsoid along a principal axis, with uniform scalar susceptibility in SI, let $H_{\mathrm{int}}=H_a-NM$ and $M=\chi H_{\mathrm{int}}$. Then

$$\chi_{\mathrm{app}}=\frac{M}{H_a}=\frac{\chi}{1+N\chi}.$$

Shielding and expulsion can differ because of field history, geometry, connectivity and pinning. ## Discovery implications

Build a magnetic evidence package around discriminating measurements: cooling history for trapping, dimensions and orientation for demagnetization, thickness for sheet response, and transport or heat capacity on comparable specimens for complementary evidence. Preserve disagreements between probes until sample and analysis differences are tested.

Separate measured magnetic response, the fitted electrodynamic parameters and the microscopic interpretation. This keeps magnetic evidence useful for discovering superconductivity without turning one model-dependent inversion into an unqualified material property or mechanism assignment.

articles.body:
## Scope

Heat capacity probes the change of entropy with temperature. A superconducting anomaly can therefore provide a bulk thermodynamic check that complements resistance and magnetic screening. A peak alone does not identify its cause: magnetic, structural and charge-order transitions can also produce anomalies. This article separates an ideal electronic heat-capacity jump from the measured total signal and from an empirical trend across different samples.

Use $C$ on a declared basis: per mole, per unit mass, per volume or for the entire sample. The normalization of the normal-state electronic coefficient $\gamma_n$ must match. Experiments often measure $C_p$, while a simple electronic model evaluates heat capacity with a fixed spectrum and volume. Their difference may be small for an appropriate low-temperature solid, but that approximation should be justified when quantitative precision matters.

## Mathematical assumptions

For an isotropic single-band weak-coupling BCS model with a smooth density of states, define the electronic jump on cooling as $\Delta C_e=C_{es}(T_c^-)-C_{en}(T_c^+)$. Its limiting value is

$$
\frac{\Delta C_e}{\gamma_nT_c}=\frac{12}{7\zeta(3)}\simeq1.426.
$$

Here $C_{en}=\gamma_nT$ in the assumed low-temperature normal state. The number is a model benchmark, not a threshold that every superconductor must pass. Johnston gives the limiting expression in Eq. (22) of the cited author manuscript. [R1](#ref-source-85009580cf550887)

Entropy follows from $dS=C\,dT/T$ under the specified thermodynamic constraints. For a continuous transition with equal extrapolated zero-temperature entropies in the compared phases,

$$
S_s(T_c)-S_n(T_c)=\int_0^{T_c}\frac{C_s(T)-C_n(T)}{T}\,dT=0.
$$

The normal curve below $T_c$ is a defined reference, not a directly accessible zero-field equilibrium phase. Background subtraction and low-temperature extrapolation therefore affect the test. A first-order transition has latent heat and requires a different treatment. Do not force this continuous-transition construction onto such a dataset.

An independent numerical check for this entry solved the constant-density-of-states gap equation, integrated the quasiparticle entropy and differentiated it near $T_c$. The normalized jump approaches 1.426 as the cutoff and numerical step are controlled; the normalized entropy reaches the normal-state value at the transition. This checks the stated model and conventions, not a material dataset. The entropy and heat-capacity relations are consistent with the selected manuscript equations. [R1](#ref-source-85009580cf550887)

## Experimental criteria

Start from the measured heat capacity and report addenda, sample mass and calibration uncertainty. A fit such as $C_n/T=\gamma_n+\beta T^2$ assumes a linear electronic term and a low-temperature lattice contribution. It can fail if extra excitations or nearby transitions matter. State the temperature interval and uncertainty of the background, and show how another reasonable background changes the inferred anomaly.

A field used to suppress superconductivity is not automatically a perfect normal-state reference. Check whether it reaches the normal state over the relevant range and whether it changes magnetic or other contributions. Use the same units and sample basis in the field and zero-field curves. Show transition width, the chosen thermodynamic $T_c$ and the entropy comparison, rather than only a peak height.

Compare with resistance and screening on the same or demonstrably comparable specimen. A consistent anomaly with the expected field response strengthens the case for bulk superconductivity. Failure to resolve an anomaly may instead reflect sensitivity, sample size, a small superconducting fraction or an incorrect baseline. It leaves thermodynamic confirmation incomplete; it does not by itself establish absence of superconductivity. These are reporting and interpretation criteria from the pinned chapter, not independently verified measurements.

## Limits and disputes

The phenomenological alpha model retains the BCS normalized gap shape while varying $\alpha=\Delta(0)/(k_BT_c)$ in the thermodynamic calculation. Padamsee and colleagues describe its quasiparticle construction in their abstract. A successful fit is not a microscopic derivation of the interaction. [R2](#ref-source-456cad7bcd596be8)

Within that model the jump scales as $1.426(\alpha/\alpha_{\rm BCS})^2$. This does not mean that the entire entropy or heat-capacity curve can simply be multiplied by that factor: the occupation functions also change. Gap anisotropy or multiple coupled bands can alter the normalized jump. Multiple bands do not necessarily broaden a single sharp transition; disorder, phase mixtures and a distribution of local transition temperatures are separate issues. [R1](#ref-source-85009580cf550887)

Bud'ko, Ni and Canfield report an empirical relation $\Delta C_p/T_c\propto T_c^2$ for their substituted Ba122 series together with specified literature samples. Equivalently, the jump itself scales as $T_c^3$ within that comparison. This is a dataset-dependent observation, not a fundamental law or a stand-alone proof of a pairing mechanism. The current check covers the publisher abstract, not a reanalysis of the data. [R3](#ref-source-f075b0cef0106abc)

## Discovery implications

Use an anomaly to constrain a proposed state together with independent probes. Ask which part of the temperature dependence is reliable, how much of the sample participates, and whether competing backgrounds could produce the same result. Preserve disagreement between probes and the uncertainty in extrapolated quantities.

A useful next experiment resolves a specific ambiguity: a field-dependent background, an uncertain phase fraction, a residual low-temperature term or an alternative gap distribution. Comparing a single normalized jump to 1.426 cannot uniquely select gap symmetry, coupling strength or a mediator. These are model-discrimination questions, not new experimental findings.

## Related topics

Connect heat capacity to [zero resistance](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [the Meissner effect](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [critical fields](/scwiki/critical-fields), [the BCS baseline](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), and [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing).

Entropy follows from $dS=C\,dT/T$ under the specified thermodynamic constraints. For a continuous transition with equal extrapolated zero-temperature entropies in the compared phases,

$$
S_s(T_c)-S_n(T_c)=\int_0^{T_c}\frac{C_s(T)-C_n(T)}{T}\,dT=0.

The normal curve below $T_c$ is a defined reference, not a directly accessible zero-field equilibrium phase. Background subtraction and low-temperature extrapolation therefore affect the test. A first-order transition has latent heat and requires a different treatment. Do not force this continuous-transition construction onto such a dataset.

This checks the stated model and conventions, not a material dataset. The entropy and heat-capacity relations are consistent with the selected manuscript equations. ## Experimental criteria

Start from the measured heat capacity and report addenda, sample mass and calibration uncertainty. A fit such as $C_n/T=\gamma_n+\beta T^2$ assumes a linear electronic term and a low-temperature lattice contribution. It can fail if extra excitations or nearby transitions matter. State the temperature interval and uncertainty of the background, and show how another reasonable background changes the inferred anomaly.

A field used to suppress superconductivity is not automatically a perfect normal-state reference. Check whether it reaches the normal state over the relevant range and whether it changes magnetic or other contributions. Use the same units and sample basis in the field and zero-field curves. Show transition width, the chosen thermodynamic $T_c$ and the entropy comparison, rather than only a peak height.

Compare with resistance and screening on the same or demonstrably comparable specimen. A consistent anomaly with the expected field response strengthens the case for bulk superconductivity. Failure to resolve an anomaly may instead reflect sensitivity, sample size, a small superconducting fraction or an incorrect baseline. It leaves thermodynamic confirmation incomplete; it does not by itself establish absence of superconductivity. These are reporting and interpretation criteria from the pinned chapter, not independently verified measurements.

## Limits and disputes

The phenomenological alpha model retains the BCS normalized gap shape while varying $\alpha=\Delta(0)/(k_BT_c)$ in the thermodynamic calculation. Padamsee and colleagues describe its quasiparticle construction in their abstract. A successful fit is not a microscopic derivation of the interaction. [R2](#ref-source-456cad7bcd596be8)

Within that model the jump scales as $1.426(\alpha/\alpha_{\rm BCS})^2$. This does not mean that the entire entropy or heat-capacity curve can simply be multiplied by that factor: the occupation functions also change. Gap anisotropy or multiple coupled bands can alter the normalized jump. Multiple bands do not necessarily broaden a single sharp transition; disorder, phase mixtures and a distribution of local transition temperatures are separate issues. [R1](#ref-source-85009580cf550887)

Bud'ko, Ni and Canfield report an empirical relation $\Delta C_p/T_c\propto T_c^2$ for their substituted Ba122 series together with specified literature samples. Equivalently, the jump itself scales as $T_c^3$ within that comparison. This is a dataset-dependent observation, not a fundamental law or a stand-alone proof of a pairing mechanism. The current check covers the publisher abstract, not a reanalysis of the data. [R3](#ref-source-f075b0cef0106abc)

## Discovery implications

Use an anomaly to constrain a proposed state together with independent probes. Ask which part of the temperature dependence is reliable, how much of the sample participates, and whether competing backgrounds could produce the same result. Preserve disagreement between probes and the uncertainty in extrapolated quantities.

A useful next experiment resolves a specific ambiguity: a field-dependent background, an uncertain phase fraction, a residual low-temperature term or an alternative gap distribution. Comparing a single normalized jump to 1.426 cannot uniquely select gap symmetry, coupling strength or a mediator. These are model-discrimination questions, not new experimental findings.

articles.body:
## Scope

Isotope substitution changes nuclear mass while keeping the element the same. The resulting response of a transition temperature can constrain lattice involvement, provided the compared samples have controlled chemistry and structure. It does not, by itself, identify the complete pairing interaction. This entry distinguishes a mass derivative, a finite comparison between samples and a microscopic explanation.

The classic mercury reports by Maxwell and Reynolds and colleagues, and Fröhlich's early theory paper, are historical starting points. Their bibliographic identities are checked here; their original experimental curves and derivations are not. No mercury exponent is extracted from those metadata records. [R3](#ref-source-eff5a2a1c455e7f6) [R4](#ref-source-e8a489943f13c9f8) [R5](#ref-source-51114e33276df5b9)

## Mathematical assumptions

For element $i$, with other masses and specified sample conditions held fixed, define

$$\alpha_i=-\frac{\partial\ln T_c}{\partial\ln M_i},\qquad \widehat\alpha_i=-\frac{\ln(T_{c,2}/T_{c,1})}{\ln(M_{i,2}/M_{i,1})}.$$

The finite estimate averages a slope over the chosen interval; it equals the local derivative only for an appropriate limiting interval or a power law. Use the mean mass implied by measured isotope abundances, not automatically an integer isotope label. A partial coefficient is not the total $\alpha_{\rm tot}=\sum_i\alpha_i$. This sum describes a common logarithmic scaling of all component masses under the same constraints. [R2](#ref-source-60ffd9b4ef2c9ccd)

For a harmonic mode with fixed force constant, $\omega\propto M^{-1/2}$. If the transition scale is proportional to that frequency and all dimensionless interaction parameters remain mass independent, differentiation gives $\alpha=1/2$. The fixed-parameter condition is essential. A measured deviation challenges that restricted model, not every possible electron–phonon theory. [R2](#ref-source-60ffd9b4ef2c9ccd)

An illustrative two-mass optical oscillator makes the distinction concrete. If $\omega^2=K(1/M_1+1/M_2)$ and $T_c\propto\omega$, direct differentiation gives

$$\alpha_1=\frac{M_2}{2(M_1+M_2)},\qquad \alpha_2=\frac{M_1}{2(M_1+M_2)},\qquad \alpha_1+\alpha_2=\frac12.$$

Each partial coefficient can be below one half even in this harmonic construction. These equations are a local illustrative derivation, checked against numerical mass derivatives; they are not a fit to MgB2 or a microscopic pairing calculation.

For uncertainty propagation let $N=\ln(T_{c,2}/T_{c,1})$ and $D=\ln(M_{i,2}/M_{i,1})$. First-order propagation for $\widehat\alpha=-N/D$ gives

$$\sigma_\alpha^2\simeq\frac{\operatorname{Var}(N)}{D^2}+\frac{N^2\operatorname{Var}(D)}{D^4}-\frac{2N\operatorname{Cov}(N,D)}{D^3}.$$

This linear approximation requires small uncertainties relative to the resolved mass interval. Shared calibration errors can be correlated; treating all temperatures as independent can misstate the uncertainty. The analytic gradient was checked against finite differences. Those arithmetic checks do not establish experimental precision.

## Experimental criteria

Bud'ko and colleagues report MgB2 isotope samples with magnetic onsets at 40.2 K for boron-10 and 39.2 K for boron-11. They use 25 G, warming after zero-field cooling, and a 2% onset of the low-temperature diamagnetic signal. Heat capacity also shows the shift. Their reported boron coefficient is $0.26\pm0.03$, a partial coefficient. Using nominal masses 10 and 11 gives about 0.264 from the stated temperatures; this only checks arithmetic, not enrichment or their error estimate. [R1](#ref-source-22ad55507a1e49c5)

A separate study by Hinks, Claus and Jorgensen measures both components. Its author manuscript reports partial coefficients of $0.30(1)$ for boron and $0.02(1)$ for magnesium, with total $0.32(1)$. Its magnetic protocol uses 1 G and compares extrapolated onset with a 10% criterion. These values belong to that study and must not be assembled from unrelated samples or criteria. The authors explicitly discuss possible impurity effects in their magnesium comparison. [R2](#ref-source-60ffd9b4ef2c9ccd)

For a new comparison, report enrichment, composition, structure, defects, preparation history and the exact temperature criterion. Characterize spectral frequency shifts where feasible. Back-exchange can test reversibility, but annealing itself may change the specimen. Repeat controls and uncertainty estimates are needed before assigning a shift exclusively to mass. These are editorial reporting recommendations, not claims that every cited study performed every control.

## Limits and disputes

A small response for one element does not exclude its contribution to a coupled vibrational system. Conversely, a nonzero response does not reconstruct the full electron–phonon spectral function or uniquely determine a mediator. Mass-dependent interactions, anharmonicity and structural changes require explicit models; the sign or size alone cannot settle them. The cited Hinks manuscript discusses alternatives to its own interaction-parameter interpretation. [R2](#ref-source-60ffd9b4ef2c9ccd)

Do not merge resistive onset, zero resistance, magnetic screening and a calorimetric transition into one unqualified temperature. The material records below preserve the magnetic criterion actually checked. Pressure and equilibrium classifications not established in the selected passages remain unknown. Comparing isotope coefficients from different studies also requires their sample preparation and systematic uncertainties.

## Discovery implications

Ask which controlled observation would separate a direct mass dependence from a changed sample. Joint measurements of structure, composition, vibrational spectra and independent superconducting probes can narrow the interpretation. Preserve null results and disagreements rather than treating the isotope exponent as a pass/fail label.

A quantitative theory should predict the response of the same observable under the same substitution and constraints. Agreement with one coefficient is a consistency check; a credible explanation must also confront the remaining measurements. These are model-discrimination criteria, not a new material discovery.

## Related topics

Read the [BCS baseline](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), [heat-capacity evidence](/scwiki/specific-heat-jump), [Meissner screening](/scwiki/meissner-effect), and [zero resistance](/scwiki/zero-resistance) alongside an isotope comparison.

This linear approximation requires small uncertainties relative to the resolved mass interval. Bud'ko and colleagues report MgB2 isotope samples with magnetic onsets at 40.2 K for boron-10 and 39.2 K for boron-11. They use 25 G, warming after zero-field cooling, and a 2% onset of the low-temperature diamagnetic signal. Heat capacity also shows the shift. Using nominal masses 10 and 11 gives about 0.264 from the stated temperatures; this only checks arithmetic, not enrichment or their error estimate.

For a new comparison, report enrichment, composition, structure, defects, preparation history and the exact temperature criterion. Characterize spectral frequency shifts where feasible. A small response for one element does not exclude its contribution to a coupled vibrational system. Mass-dependent interactions, anharmonicity and structural changes require explicit models; the sign or size alone cannot settle them. The cited Hinks manuscript discusses alternatives to its own interaction-parameter interpretation.

articles.body:
## Scope

A superconducting gap is an energy scale in a specified excitation spectrum. Its magnitude, momentum dependence and relative phase answer different questions. A suppression of spectral weight is not automatically a superconducting gap, and a fitted gap does not automatically define the temperature of bulk superconductivity. This entry organizes observations and model assumptions rather than ranking materials by a single gap ratio.

Specify whether $\Delta$ denotes an order-parameter amplitude, a quasiparticle excitation threshold or a parameter extracted from a broadened spectrum. The relation between these quantities depends on the model. Keep the measured signal, the fit and the inferred state separate; otherwise apparently similar numbers can describe different observables.

## Mathematical assumptions

For a clean, isotropic, single-band weak-coupling BCS model, the quasiparticle spectrum and zero-temperature limiting ratio are

$$E_{\mathbf k}=\sqrt{\xi_{\mathbf k}^{\,2}+|\Delta|^2},\qquad \frac{2\Delta_0}{k_BT_c}=2\pi e^{-\gamma_E}\simeq3.528.$$

Here $\xi_{\mathbf k}$ is measured from the chemical potential and $\gamma_E$ is Euler's constant. The existing BCS entry checks the gap equation and numerical limit. The ratio is not a universal threshold for identifying superconductivity or an interaction. Strong coupling and anisotropy require their own treatment; Carbotte's review abstract describes deviations from simple BCS results without supplying a universal correction. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R2](#ref-source-2da854ce10895b5e)

With a constant normal density of states $N_n$ and the same spin convention in numerator and denominator, the ideal normalized density of states at positive excitation energy is

$$\frac{N_s(E)}{N_n}=\begin{cases}0,&0\le E<|\Delta|,\\ E/\sqrt{E^2-|\Delta|^2},&E>|\Delta|.\end{cases}$$

The factor above the edge follows from the change of variable $E=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2}$ with the usual Bogoliubov spectral weights. The ideal edge is singular but integrable. A local numerical check integrates it up to a finite energy and recovers the corresponding normal-state $\xi$ interval. The check assumes no lifetime broadening, gap anisotropy or experimental convolution. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

In this magnitude-only model, replacing a gap by its negative leaves the excitation energies unchanged. Likewise, independently summing two uncoupled spectral contributions cannot recover their relative sign. This is a limited counterexample to inferring phase from a gap magnitude; it does not say that every interference-sensitive spectrum is phase blind.

## Experimental criteria

Use the following as a reporting map adapted from the pinned chapter. Each interpretation needs the stated model and a sample-specific source; these rows do not certify any material dataset.

| Probe | Recorded quantity | What must be controlled |
|---|---|---|
| Tunneling or STS | Differential conductance versus bias | Tip and sample spectra, thermal/instrumental broadening, matrix elements and surface variation |
| ARPES | Momentum-resolved photoemission intensity | Occupation, resolution, matrix elements and surface state; a leading edge is not automatically a gap amplitude |
| Optical or THz spectroscopy | Frequency-dependent electrodynamic response | Scattering, multiple bands and the model linking absorption to an excitation threshold |
| Heat capacity | Entropy and bulk excitation contribution | Lattice/magnetic backgrounds and normalization; no direct phase measurement |
| Penetration depth or thermal transport | Low-energy electromagnetic or heat response | Disorder, nonlocality, background and multiple excitation channels |
| Andreev or point-contact spectroscopy | Interface current and conductance | Barrier transparency, heating, contact regime and channel mixing |

A tunnel conductance resembles the sample density of states only with suitable assumptions about the counterelectrode and tunneling matrix element, and after accounting for the thermal convolution. Do not identify every conductance peak with $\Delta$. Photoemission and thermodynamic measurements constrain different aspects of the state; the selected review discusses why magnitude-sensitive probes alone do not measure the relative phase. [R3](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

Hardy and colleagues report a strong linear term in the penetration-depth change of YBa2Cu3O6.95 single crystals over approximately 3–25 K using a 900 MHz resonator. This is evidence relevant to low-energy excitations under their sample conditions, not a direct measurement of gap phase. The present check covers the publisher abstract. [R4](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

By contrast, Tsuei and Kirtley use scanning SQUID measurements of NCCO/PCCO tricrystals to test phase-sensitive predictions. Their designed frustrated geometry produces a half-flux signal, while two unfrustrated NCCO geometries serve as controls. The inference depends on junction geometry and the associated model, not merely on observing a spectral dip. Selected author-manuscript passages and the control description were checked; the image fits were not independently reproduced. [R6](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Nodes, relative sign and topology are distinct. A low-temperature power law can constrain low-energy excitations without uniquely selecting a pairing representation. A fully open gap on each Fermi-surface sheet can coexist with a relative sign change between sheets. Disorder and sample inhomogeneity must be considered before translating a temperature dependence into a symmetry assignment. [R3](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

A zero-bias feature alone is not a unique topology test. Identify its field, temperature, position and junction dependence, then compare explicit alternative models. Likewise, a spectroscopic gap-closing temperature must not silently replace a resistive or thermodynamic $T_c$ in a gap ratio. These are inference and reporting limits, not a claim that one alternative explains every observed feature.

Choi and colleagues' MgB2 result is an anisotropic Eliashberg calculation of distinct band-dependent gap scales. Treat those calculated gaps as theory and compare them with separately identified measurements. The pinned chapter's DOI was mismatched; the correct source is nature00898. That correction does not validate a universal multiband gap ratio or independently reproduce the calculation. [R5](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221)

## Discovery implications

Record the specimen, pressure or strain, temperature criterion, spectral resolution, fit model and uncertainty together. Compare probes on the same or demonstrably comparable specimens. A disagreement can expose a surface effect, background assumption or a second energy scale; it should remain visible until tested.

A useful next measurement distinguishes competing interpretations. Establish which observation would separate a change of magnitude from a change of phase, and which control would rule out a contact artifact or another ordered state. Gap measurements constrain models; they do not replace a complete evidence chain for superconductivity.

## Related topics

Connect to [BCS theory](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [specific heat](/scwiki/specific-heat-jump), [critical fields](/scwiki/critical-fields), and [zero resistance](/scwiki/zero-resistance).

## Limits and disputes

Nodes, relative sign and topology are distinct. A low-temperature power law can constrain low-energy excitations without uniquely selecting a pairing representation. A fully open gap on each Fermi-surface sheet can coexist with a relative sign change between sheets. Disorder and sample inhomogeneity must be considered before translating a temperature dependence into a symmetry assignment. [R3](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

A zero-bias feature alone is not a unique topology test. Identify its field, temperature, position and junction dependence, then compare explicit alternative models. Likewise, a spectroscopic gap-closing temperature must not silently replace a resistive or thermodynamic $T_c$ in a gap ratio. These are inference and reporting limits, not a claim that one alternative explains every observed feature.

Choi and colleagues' MgB2 result is an anisotropic Eliashberg calculation of distinct band-dependent gap scales. Treat those calculated gaps as theory and compare them with separately identified measurements. The pinned chapter's DOI was mismatched; the correct source is nature00898. That correction does not validate a universal multiband gap ratio or independently reproduce the calculation. [R5](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221)

sections.title: Discovery implications
sections.markdown:
## Discovery implications

Record the specimen, pressure or strain, temperature criterion, spectral resolution, fit model and uncertainty together. Compare probes on the same or demonstrably comparable specimens. A disagreement can expose a surface effect, background assumption or a second energy scale; it should remain visible until tested.

A useful next measurement distinguishes competing interpretations. Establish which observation would separate a change of magnitude from a change of phase, and which control would rule out a contact artifact or another ordered state. Gap measurements constrain models; they do not replace a complete evidence chain for superconductivity.

# Superconducting gap: magnitude, nodes and phase

Read gap measurements with their probe and model. Distinguish an excitation scale from evidence for nodes, relative sign or bulk superconductivity.

## Scope

A superconducting gap is an energy scale in a specified excitation spectrum. Its magnitude, momentum dependence and relative phase answer different questions. A suppression of spectral weight is not automatically a superconducting gap, and a fitted gap does not automatically define the temperature of bulk superconductivity. This entry organizes observations and model assumptions rather than ranking materials by a single gap ratio.

Specify whether $\Delta$ denotes an order-parameter amplitude, a quasiparticle excitation threshold or a parameter extracted from a broadened spectrum. The relation between these quantities depends on the model. Keep the measured signal, the fit and the inferred state separate; otherwise apparently similar numbers can describe different observables.

## Mathematical assumptions

For a clean, isotropic, single-band weak-coupling BCS model, the quasiparticle spectrum and zero-temperature limiting ratio are

$$E_{\mathbf k}=\sqrt{\xi_{\mathbf k}^{\,2}+|\Delta|^2},\qquad \frac{2\Delta_0}{k_BT_c}=2\pi e^{-\gamma_E}\simeq3.528.$$

Here $\xi_{\mathbf k}$ is measured from the chemical potential and $\gamma_E$ is Euler's constant. The existing BCS entry checks the gap equation and numerical limit. The ratio is not a universal threshold for identifying superconductivity or an interaction. Strong coupling and anisotropy require their own treatment; Carbotte's review abstract describes deviations from simple BCS results without supplying a universal correction. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R2](#ref-source-2da854ce10895b5e)

With a constant normal density of states $N_n$ and the same spin convention in numerator and denominator, the ideal normalized density of states at positive excitation energy is

$$\frac{N_s(E)}{N_n}=\begin{cases}0,&0\le E<|\Delta|,\\ E/\sqrt{E^2-|\Delta|^2},&E>|\Delta|.\end{cases}$$

The factor above the edge follows from the change of variable $E=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2}$ with the usual Bogoliubov spectral weights. The ideal edge is singular but integrable. A local numerical check integrates it up to a finite energy and recovers the corresponding normal-state $\xi$ interval. The check assumes no lifetime broadening, gap anisotropy or experimental convolution. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

In this magnitude-only model, replacing a gap by its negative leaves the excitation energies unchanged. Likewise, independently summing two uncoupled spectral contributions cannot recover their relative sign. This is a limited counterexample to inferring phase from a gap magnitude; it does not say that every interference-sensitive spectrum is phase blind.

articles.body:
## Scope

A critical field needs a physical definition. The thermodynamic field $H_c$ represents the zero-field condensation-energy density, $f_n-f_s=\mu_0H_c^2/2$. This energy scale exists for both type-I and type-II superconductors; it is not generally the field at which a type-II sample becomes normal. In the ideal bulk type-II description, $H_{c1}$ marks the equilibrium onset of the mixed state and $H_{c2}$ its upper boundary. The vortex construction distinguishes those boundaries from one thermodynamic energy scale. [R1](#ref-source-89f5503f5e470385)

Here $H$ is magnetic field strength in amperes per metre, while $B$ and $\mu_0H$ are expressed in tesla. Inside matter, $B=\mu_0(H+M)$; replacing $B$ by $\mu_0H$ requires a stated magnetization approximation. An applied-field value, an internal field and a flux density must not silently share the same symbol. The formulas below use SI conventions, rather than copying Gaussian-unit factors from historical papers.

## Mathematical assumptions

For a bulk, isotropic, single-component Ginzburg–Landau model near $T_c$, neglecting paramagnetic pair breaking, linearization gives the orbital result

$$
B_{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}=\frac{\Phi_0}{2\pi\xi^2},\qquad
\Phi_0=\frac{h}{2e},\qquad
\kappa=\frac{\lambda}{\xi}.
$$

The usual $\mu_0H_{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}$ notation uses $B\simeq\mu_0H$ near this continuous boundary when normal-state magnetic response is negligible. In the same model, $H_{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}=\sqrt{2}\kappa H_c$. The GL coherence length $\xi$ and penetration depth $\lambda$ are evaluated at the same temperature. They are not interchangeable with every microscopic pair-size or fitted length. The isotropic GL type-II boundary is $\kappa=1/\sqrt{2}$. [R1](#ref-source-89f5503f5e470385)

A useful independent check follows from the linearized kinetic operator: the lowest Landau-level energy of a pair with charge magnitude $2e$ is $\hbar(2e)B/(2m^\ast)$. Equating it to $|\alpha|$, with $\xi^2=\hbar^2/(2m^\ast|\alpha|)$, gives the flux-over-area expression above. This is a model derivation, not a measured field or an all-temperature interpolation.

For a separate, purely paramagnetic comparison at zero temperature, take an isotropic weak-coupling singlet with $g=2$, negligible spin susceptibility in the paired state, no orbital cost and no competing modulated state. Equating its condensation energy to the normal-state polarization-energy gain gives

$$
B_P=\frac{\Delta_0}{\sqrt{2}\mu_B},\qquad
\frac{B_P}{T_c}=\frac{\pi e^{-\gamma}k_B}{\sqrt{2}\mu_B}
\simeq 1.86\;\mathrm{T\,K^{-1}}.
$$

This is the Clogston–Chandrasekhar reference scale. The commonly quoted $1.84\;\mathrm{T\,K^{-1}}$ uses rounded weak-coupling gap constants; neither coefficient is an exact universal experimental bound. The numerical value here uses the same modern weak-coupling gap convention as the BCS entry. The energy comparison is supported by the cited perspective; the original Clogston paper's identity is checked, but its full text was not available in this review. [R4](#ref-source-d32df19524b2a1c8) [R5](#ref-source-b717fb1db41e9f29) [R6](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Experimental criteria

Report the probe and the rule used to locate a field line. Resistance onset, a stated percentage of the normal-state resistance and a voltage-resolution-limited zero need not coincide. Neither a magnetic irreversibility line nor a first flux-entry signal should automatically be renamed $H_{c2}$ or equilibrium $H_{c1}$. Demagnetizing geometry, surface barriers, vortex motion, pinning and inhomogeneous current paths can affect the observed signal.

Record temperature, field orientation and angular uncertainty, sample geometry, pressure where relevant, current density, sweep direction and rate, and the normal-state baseline. Compare transport with an appropriate bulk thermodynamic or magnetic measurement on comparable specimens. Preserve hysteresis and transition widths instead of choosing the most favorable boundary. These are measurement-reporting requirements from the pinned chapter, not a claim that each possible artifact is present in a particular sample.

## Limits and disputes

Werthamer–Helfand–Hohenberg theory treats orbital and spin effects within a specified microscopic approximation, including spin–orbit impurity scattering. Its publisher abstract explicitly notes that such scattering counteracts paramagnetic limiting. A fitted WHH curve therefore needs its dirty-limit, spin and scattering assumptions; merely naming the fit does not establish them. This entry's WHH check is abstract-scoped. [R2](#ref-source-16926b3817cff55d)

Multiband structure also changes extrapolation. Gurevich's dirty two-gap model allows $H_{c2}(T)$ shapes controlled by different intraband diffusivities, including deviations from the one-gap slope estimate near $T_c$. That calculation is a counterexample to treating a one-band extrapolation coefficient as universal. It does not validate an arbitrary multiband fit or supply a field value for an unmeasured sample. [R3](#ref-source-7ba854cc57960377)

Exceeding the simple Pauli estimate does not uniquely identify triplet pairing. The spin response and spin–orbit energy scales may differ from the assumed reference model; the cited Ising-superconductivity perspective discusses a concrete route to a strongly anisotropic paramagnetic response. Orbital and spin limitations must be treated together when both matter. No material-specific critical-field record or pairing assignment is introduced here. [R5](#ref-source-b717fb1db41e9f29)

## Discovery implications

Use a field measurement to discriminate between declared models. First decide whether the observation concerns an equilibrium boundary, vortex dynamics or a transport threshold. Then test orientation and temperature dependence over a range where the model applies. Retain the fitting window, parameter uncertainty and alternative descriptions, particularly when extrapolating far below the measured temperatures.

A high critical field may motivate further study, but a useful discovery argument identifies which assumption failed and which new observable could distinguish the remaining explanations. Material comparisons should keep pressure, field direction and criterion attached to each value. A large fitted field alone establishes neither a microscopic pairing mediator nor topology. This is an editorial evaluation protocol; it is not a newly verified experimental result.

## Related topics

Read about [the Meissner effect](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [zero-resistance criteria](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [the BCS baseline](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), and [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-a6-claim-scope-1

A critical field needs a physical definition. The thermodynamic field $H_c$ represents the zero-field condensation-energy density, $f_n-f_s=\mu_0H_c^2/2$. This energy scale exists for both type-I and type-II superconductors; it is not generally the field at which a type-II sample becomes normal. In the ideal bulk type-II description, $H_{c1}$ marks the equilibrium onset of the mixed state and $H_{c2}$ its upper boundary. The vortex construction distinguishes those boundaries from one thermodynamic energy scale.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-89f5503f5e470385.

Conditions: Bulk equilibrium field definitions; distinguish SI H, B and magnetization, and type-I versus type-II behavior.

Verification scope: Vortex-field distinction checked against Abrikosov pp. 975-977. Thermodynamic and SI notation are explicit editorial definitions; not an independent verification of every material.

### scwiki-a6-claim-scope-2

Here $H$ is magnetic field strength in amperes per metre, while $B$ and $\mu_0H$ are expressed in tesla. Inside matter, $B=\mu_0(H+M)$; replacing $B$ by $\mu_0H$ requires a stated magnetization approximation. An applied-field value, an internal field and a flux density must not silently share the same symbol. The formulas below use SI conventions, rather than copying Gaussian-unit factors from historical papers.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-89f5503f5e470385.

Conditions: Bulk equilibrium field definitions; distinguish SI H, B and magnetization, and type-I versus type-II behavior.

Verification scope: Vortex-field distinction checked against Abrikosov pp. 975-977. Thermodynamic and SI notation are explicit editorial definitions; not an independent verification of every material.

### scwiki-a6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

For a bulk, isotropic, single-component Ginzburg–Landau model near $T_c$, neglecting paramagnetic pair breaking, linearization gives the orbital result

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-89f5503f5e470385.

Conditions: Orbital result: isotropic single-component GL near Tc, negligible paramagnetic and normal magnetic response. Pauli result separately assumes zero-temperature weak-coupling singlet, g=2, negligible paired-state spin susceptibility and no orbital or modulated-state competition.

Verification scope: Declared GL and energy-balance model calculation checked algebraically and numerically. Source-specific passage/access scope retained; not a measurement or independent microscopic-theory reproduction.

### scwiki-a6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

The usual $\mu_0H_{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}$ notation uses $B\simeq\mu_0H$ near this continuous boundary when normal-state magnetic response is negligible. In the same model, $H_{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}=\sqrt{2}\kappa H_c$. The GL coherence length $\xi$ and penetration depth $\lambda$ are evaluated at the same temperature. They are not interchangeable with every microscopic pair-size or fitted length. The isotropic GL type-II boundary is $\kappa=1/\sqrt{2}$.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-89f5503f5e470385.

Conditions: Orbital result: isotropic single-component GL near Tc, negligible paramagnetic and normal magnetic response. Pauli result separately assumes zero-temperature weak-coupling singlet, g=2, negligible paired-state spin susceptibility and no orbital or modulated-state competition.

### scwiki-a6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

A useful independent check follows from the linearized kinetic operator: the lowest Landau-level energy of a pair with charge magnitude $2e$ is $\hbar(2e)B/(2m^\ast)$. Equating it to $|\alpha|$, with $\xi^2=\hbar^2/(2m^\ast|\alpha|)$, gives the flux-over-area expression above. This is a model derivation, not a measured field or an all-temperature interpolation.

### scwiki-a6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-5

This is the Clogston–Chandrasekhar reference scale. The commonly quoted $1.84\;\mathrm{T\,K^{-1}}$ uses rounded weak-coupling gap constants; neither coefficient is an exact universal experimental bound. The numerical value here uses the same modern weak-coupling gap convention as the BCS entry. The energy comparison is supported by the cited perspective; the original Clogston paper's identity is checked, but its full text was not available in this review.

### scwiki-a6-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Report the probe and the rule used to locate a field line. Resistance onset, a stated percentage of the normal-state resistance and a voltage-resolution-limited zero need not coincide. Neither a magnetic irreversibility line nor a first flux-entry signal should automatically be renamed $H_{c2}$ or equilibrium $H_{c1}$. Demagnetizing geometry, surface barriers, vortex motion, pinning and inhomogeneous current paths can affect the observed signal.

### scwiki-a6-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Record temperature, field orientation and angular uncertainty, sample geometry, pressure where relevant, current density, sweep direction and rate, and the normal-state baseline. Compare transport with an appropriate bulk thermodynamic or magnetic measurement on comparable specimens. Preserve hysteresis and transition widths instead of choosing the most favorable boundary. ### scwiki-a6-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Werthamer–Helfand–Hohenberg theory treats orbital and spin effects within a specified microscopic approximation, including spin–orbit impurity scattering. Its publisher abstract explicitly notes that such scattering counteracts paramagnetic limiting. A fitted WHH curve therefore needs its dirty-limit, spin and scattering assumptions; merely naming the fit does not establish them. This entry's WHH check is abstract-scoped.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-16926b3817cff55d.

Conditions: WHH abstract scope, dirty two-band model scope and specified spin response; no universal field extrapolation or pairing assignment follows.

Verification scope: WHH publisher abstract only; detailed fits and numerical theory remain unreviewed.

### scwiki-a6-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

Multiband structure also changes extrapolation. Gurevich's dirty two-gap model allows $H_{c2}(T)$ shapes controlled by different intraband diffusivities, including deviations from the one-gap slope estimate near $T_c$. That calculation is a counterexample to treating a one-band extrapolation coefficient as universal. It does not validate an arbitrary multiband fit or supply a field value for an unmeasured sample.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-7ba854cc57960377.

Conditions: WHH abstract scope, dirty two-band model scope and specified spin response; no universal field extrapolation or pairing assignment follows.

Verification scope: Gurevich abstract and introduction pp. 184515-1 to -2; no numerical solution reproduced.

### scwiki-a6-claim-limits-and-disputes-3

Exceeding the simple Pauli estimate does not uniquely identify triplet pairing. The spin response and spin–orbit energy scales may differ from the assumed reference model; the cited Ising-superconductivity perspective discusses a concrete route to a strongly anisotropic paramagnetic response. Orbital and spin limitations must be treated together when both matter. No material-specific critical-field record or pairing assignment is introduced here.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-b717fb1db41e9f29.

Conditions: WHH abstract scope, dirty two-band model scope and specified spin response; no universal field extrapolation or pairing assignment follows.

Verification scope: Wickramaratne-Mazin perspective section II, pp. 240503-2 to -3; model spin-response argument, no material-specific field or pairing validation.

### scwiki-a6-claim-discovery-implications-1

Use a field measurement to discriminate between declared models. First decide whether the observation concerns an equilibrium boundary, vortex dynamics or a transport threshold. Then test orientation and temperature dependence over a range where the model applies. Retain the fitting window, parameter uncertainty and alternative descriptions, particularly when extrapolating far below the measured temperatures.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-7ba854cc57960377.

Conditions: Editorial model-discrimination protocol; no measured critical-field values or established pairing mechanisms are asserted.

Verification scope: Editorial reporting protocol adapted from pinned A6 chapter, not independently verified experimental findings. Cited theory motivates distinctions only; it does not certify each measurement artifact.

### scwiki-a6-claim-discovery-implications-2

A high critical field may motivate further study, but a useful discovery argument identifies which assumption failed and which new observable could distinguish the remaining explanations. Material comparisons should keep pressure, field direction and criterion attached to each value. A large fitted field alone establishes neither a microscopic pairing mediator nor topology. This is an editorial evaluation protocol; it is not a newly verified experimental result.

articles.body:
## Scope

Critical current is a limit defined for a specimen, measurement protocol and operating conditions. Transport measurements use a voltage or electric-field criterion; magnetization measurements infer a current through a model; the depairing current describes loss of stability of a superconducting state within a specified theory. These quantities must not share an unlabeled performance ranking.

Blatter and colleagues explicitly distinguish depinning and depairing current densities in their review abstract. Pinning, thermal fluctuations and vortex motion affect practical current transport. A measured threshold can instead be limited by weak connections or heating; its mechanism requires evidence beyond the value of the current itself. [R2](#ref-source-82f53ca35625217d)

## Mathematical assumptions

|---|---|---|

| Magnetization | Magnetic moment, volume, dimensions, field history, sweep rate, elapsed time and background subtraction | Conversion to current requires a geometry and critical-state model |
| Conductor or cable | Superconducting fraction, whole-conductor area, length, strain and thermal stabilization | Layer current density and engineering current density answer different questions |
| Depairing model | Model, temperature regime, geometry and stability assumptions | A calculated instability is not automatically the measured transport limit |

MacManus-Driscoll and colleagues studied YBCO films grown with BaZrO3 added to the target. Their selected manuscript passages report improved in-field transport at 75.5 K, despite lower transition temperature or self-field current in some samples. The rotated field remained perpendicular to current. This comparison illustrates distinct performance measures, not proof of a different pairing mechanism. Larbalestier and colleagues' 2014 paper is a primary Bi-2212 round-wire study, not a general engineering review. An irreversible magnetic response and the upper critical field are different observables. [R3](#ref-source-51c947cf11bea72e)

Separate a better transport path, stronger pinning, a larger superconducting fraction and a higher depairing limit as distinct hypotheses. Compare controlled specimens under matched conditions before assigning an improvement to a microscopic mechanism. A gain in current-carrying performance does not by itself demonstrate higher $T_c$, a new pairing interaction or a new superconducting phase.

Preserve the measured signal, uncertainty and analysis conventions together. If the voltage criterion, geometry or thermal history is unavailable, retain that gap in the record. A useful follow-up is the measurement that discriminates between the competing limits, rather than another unsupported performance ranking.

articles.body:
## Scope

Linear-temperature resistivity describes a measured dependence over a specified range. The fit $\rho(T)=\rho_0+AT$ needs a sample, current direction, field, temperature interval and residuals. A straight-looking trace is not by itself evidence for a quantum critical point, a universal lifetime or a pairing interaction. This entry treats transport phenomenology; the linked Planckian entry discusses lifetime interpretations.

Separate a finite-field normal state, the region affected by superconducting fluctuations, and a higher-temperature regime that may have different scattering. Martin and colleagues' Bi-based crystal abstract reports strongly anisotropic transport; an in-plane trend is not an isotropic resistivity law. [R1](#ref-source-a5d6480d08ee8555)

## Mathematical assumptions

A least-squares slope depends on both the model and the sampled window. For exact synthetic data $\rho=r_0+aT+bT^2$, equally weighted temperatures symmetric about $\bar T$ give

$$A_{\mathrm{fit}}=a+2b\bar T.$$

This follows by inserting the quadratic into $\operatorname{cov}(T,\rho)/\operatorname{var}(T)$. A narrower interval can hide curvature while changing the inferred slope. Independent synthetic fits confirm this counterexample; they are not fits to any material. Experimental model comparison also needs uncertainties, correlations and a justified treatment of residuals.

For a single isotropic Drude channel with temperature-independent carrier density $n$ and mass $m^*$, an inelastic pole relaxation rate $\gamma=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$ gives $A=\alpha m^*k_B/(ne^2\hbar)$. Thus a slope fixes $\alpha$ only after the carrier parameters and response model are specified. If those parameters change with temperature, differentiating resistivity produces additional terms. This conditional connection underlies the selected Legros analysis. [R4](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

For a circular, parabolic two-dimensional band with total degeneracy $g$, use total sheet density $n_{2D}=gk_F^2/(4\pi)$ and $k_BT_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/(2m^*)$. The preceding Drude model then yields

$$A_{\square}T_F=\frac{\alpha h}{g e^2}.$$

The familiar factor of two corresponds to $g=2$, not an arbitrary multiband system. A bulk slope converted per conducting plane uses $A_{\square}=A/d$ with the stated effective plane spacing $d$. Independent occupied-disk and algebra checks cover $g=1,2,4$; neither degeneracy nor a mass should be transferred between materials without justification.

Parallel channels add conductivities. As an independent scalar, zero-field example, let $r(T)=r_0+aT>0$ describe one channel and let $\sigma_b\ge0$ be a constant background conductivity in matching units. Then

$$\rho_{\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{r(T)}{1+\sigma_b r(T)},\qquad\frac{d\rho_{\mathrm{tot}}}{dT}=\frac{a}{[1+\sigma_b r(T)]^2}.$$

The total slope is generally temperature dependent even though the first channel's resistance is exactly linear. Nine numerical derivative checks verify this model. It is not a multiband fit; in magnetic field, conductivity tensors must be added before inversion. Adding scattering mechanisms within one channel is a different assumption from adding parallel conductivities.

## Experimental criteria

Legros and colleagues' earlier manuscript measures a Bi2212 film with nominal hole doping 0.23 in pulsed fields. Its 55 T trace and magnetoresistance-corrected, extrapolated zero-field curve are distinct datasets. The analysis estimates carrier parameters and geometric uncertainty; the checked passages do not turn its interpretation into a model-independent universal bound. [R4](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

Cao and colleagues measure four-probe transport in gated twisted bilayer graphene. Their linear regime depends on filling and a crossover temperature. The operational scattering coefficient uses density and mass from low-temperature quantum oscillations; those assumptions matter when interpreting higher-temperature transport. The selected passages do not establish one shared microscopic mechanism across material families. [R5](#ref-source-8135909144b6b16b)

Romero and colleagues' earlier manuscript studies two 100 nm FeTe1-xSex films, x = 0.45 and 0.35, over 0.2–3 THz. Its narrow-channel fits use 20–40 K and report coefficients 3.02 and 2.42 in $\Gamma=\Gamma_0+\alpha k_BT/h$. These are channel-specific fit results, not coefficients of the total DC resistivity. [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Record the raw voltage/current or conductivity data, geometry, composition, field direction, fit interval and uncertainty model. Identify excluded transition regions and test alternative fit windows and curvature. A successful fit does not establish that its parameters are uniquely identifiable. Normal-state measurement temperatures remain separate from superconducting transition temperatures in the records below.

## Limits and disputes

Frequency conventions can create a factor-of-$2\pi$ error. For a Drude denominator $\Gamma-i\nu$ with ordinary frequency $\nu$, the corresponding pole rate is $\gamma=1/\tau=2\pi\Gamma$ in a denominator $\gamma-i\omega$, where $\omega=2\pi\nu$. Consequently $\Gamma=\alpha k_BT/h$ converts to $\gamma=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$. State the denominator and linewidth convention before comparing coefficients. This is a convention check, not a new measurement of a lifetime.

A shared temperature exponent does not identify a unique microscopic interaction. Drude transport, optical fits and single-particle lifetimes measure or infer different quantities. Extrapolating carrier parameters, suppressing superconductivity by field, or neglecting a parallel channel can affect an inferred coefficient. Report these choices alongside any claimed universality rather than treating the fit exponent as a proof.

Cooper's LSCO study and Bruin's cross-metal comparison remain bibliographic starting points here. Their complete datasets and numerical conclusions have not been reanalyzed in this entry. Selected manuscript checks above also leave final-version comparison and full uncertainty reproduction open. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225) [R3](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae)

## Discovery implications

Use linear-T transport to organize experiments, not to rank superconductors or predict a transition temperature by itself. A stronger comparison holds sample state, probe definition and fitting procedure fixed, then asks whether independent optical, thermodynamic or quantum-oscillation information supports the same parameter interpretation. Retain counterexamples and failed fits; correlation with superconductivity does not identify its cause.

## Related topics

Continue with [Planckian dissipation](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation), [zero resistance](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [critical fields](/scwiki/critical-fields), [specific heat](/scwiki/specific-heat-jump), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), and [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing).

Frequency conventions can create a factor-of-$2\pi$ error.
