articles.body:
## Scope

Resonating valence bond, or RVB, denotes a family of correlated-state constructions built from quantum superpositions of singlet bonds. Anderson's 1987 proposal connected singlets in a correlated insulator to superconductivity after doping. It is a theoretical route, not a diagnosis obtained merely by finding a superconductor near an insulator. The original article's indexed abstract was checked; its complete argument remains outside this source review. [R1](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0)

RVB is not synonymous with a particular quantum spin liquid, a universal pairing boson or a directly measurable order parameter. A chosen wavefunction, projection and treatment of emergent gauge dynamics determine its physical predictions. The Lee–Nagaosa–Wen formulation distinguishes the redundancy used to represent electrons from the low-energy gauge structure of a state. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

## Mathematical assumptions

A singlet on ordered sites $i,j$ is $|s_{ij}\rangle=(|\uparrow_i\downarrow_j\rangle-|\downarrow_i\uparrow_j\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Different products of such bonds need not be orthogonal. An independent four-spin illustration takes $A=|s_{12}s_{34}\rangle$ and $B=|s_{14}s_{23}\rangle$, with the stated orientation fixing their relative sign. Direct expansion gives $\langle A|B\rangle=-1/2$, so the normalized superposition is $(A-B)/\sqrt3$, not $(A-B)/\sqrt2$.

For the periodic four-site spin Hamiltonian $H=J\sum_{i=1}^4\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_{i+1}$ with $J>0$, direct action on this superposition gives energy $-2J$ and zero eigenvector residual. An equal incoherent mixture of the two bond coverings has energy $-3J/2$. The difference demonstrates quantum interference in a specified finite spin problem. Neither result establishes bulk topological order or superconductivity: this model has no mobile charge degrees of freedom.

To distinguish a strong-coupling approximation from an exact scale, consider a two-site, one-orbital Hubbard model with two electrons, hopping $t$ and repulsion $U>0$. Exact diagonalization of its six-state sector gives a singlet–triplet splitting

$$J_{\mathrm{dimer}}=\frac{\sqrt{U^2+16t^2}-U}{2}\simeq\frac{4t^2}{U}\quad(U\gg|t|).$$

Four independent matrix calculations agree with the exact expression. At $U/|t|=4$, the leading expression overestimates the splitting by about 20.7%; at 32 the error is about 0.39%. The local exchange scale and its expansion do not by themselves predict a pairing temperature in a doped lattice. Multiorbital charge-transfer materials require additional assumptions before using this one-band reduction.

A projected-electron construction writes $c_{i\sigma}=b_i^\dagger f_{i\sigma}$ with $b_i^\dagger b_i+\sum_\sigma f_{i\sigma}^\dagger f_{i\sigma}=1$. It represents the reduced local Hilbert space containing an empty site and two singly occupied spin states. Under the internal redundancy $f_i\to e^{i\theta_i}f_i$, $b_i\to e^{i\theta_i}b_i$, the electron remains invariant. A spinon pair alone changes phase; the accompanying charge factor cancels it. Three explicit phase checks confirm this cancellation. A gauge-fixed factorization into spin and charge averages is an approximation, not separate observation of either factor. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

An independent Gaussian response illustration minimizes

$$F(a,A)=\frac{\rho_b}{2}(A-a)^2+\frac{\rho_f}{2}a^2,\qquad \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\rho_b\rho_f}{\rho_b+\rho_f}.$$

Here $A$ is a normalized external field, $a$ an internal field, and nonnegative coefficients describe two sectors within this quadratic model. Four direct minimizations agree with the expression. A finite $\rho_f$ does not provide charged stiffness when $\rho_b=0$. This is a restricted response illustration: non-Gaussian and compact gauge fluctuations are absent, and it is not a universal experimental law.

## Experimental criteria

Establish the insulating state's magnetic and structural properties before naming it a spin liquid. Vaknin and colleagues' neutron-diffraction study of undoped La2CuO4-y reports magnetic superlattice evidence for antiferromagnetism. That parent-state observation must be retained alongside the historical RVB proposal. A measured superconducting gap symmetry may constrain candidate states without uniquely selecting their microscopic explanation. [R7](#ref-source-9dda11fbf0c41f73)

Lefebvre and colleagues mapped kappa-(ET)2Cu[N(CN)2]Cl using helium pressure, proton NMR and ac susceptibility. The selected manuscript uses a 0.5 T field for NMR and no static field for the susceptibility measurement; it restricts hydrostatic sweeps to conditions above helium solidification. The authors report inhomogeneous phase coexistence but do not resolve whether it is macroscopic or mesoscopic. These conditions belong to kappa-Cl and cannot be transferred to a different organic salt. [R3](#ref-source-2cc5358d54a65217)

For kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3, Shimizu and colleagues' abstract reports no NMR indication of long-range order down to 32 mK, despite a susceptibility-derived exchange scale around 250 K. Neither number is a superconducting transition temperature. Kurosaki and colleagues separately studied its pressure-dependent NMR and resistivity phase diagram. The existence of neighboring superconductivity does not identify the insulating state's excitations as its pairing mechanism. Those two sources remain abstract-scoped here. [R4](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R5](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c)

## Limits and disputes

Pustogow and colleagues' 2023 strain-transport study favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic candidate's 6 K anomaly. The 140 nm crystal is coupled to a PET substrate; quoted hydrostatic-equivalent pressures are inferred by comparison with transport data. The paper acknowledges that a gapped chiral spin liquid is not ruled out without a discriminating experiment. It also assigns sharp resistance jumps to mounting-related microcracks. A transport anomaly or phase-diagram shape alone must not be promoted to an unambiguous microscopic spin-state determination. [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

The Lee–Nagaosa–Wen review itself notes an experimental mismatch in the doping dependence of the Gaussian U(1) prediction for the temperature slope of superfluid density. Thus the simple response construction above has an explicit historical limitation. Naming a redundant representation U(1), SU(2) or Z2 is not sufficient to establish the corresponding emergent low-energy phase. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

Pseudogaps, Fermi arcs, singlet correlations and d-wave pairing each admit more than one theoretical description. Test a specified RVB state against physical correlation functions, charge stiffness, spectral weight, symmetry and disorder responses. Treating all these observations as interchangeable proof would remove the very distinctions needed to compare mechanisms. Full final-version, data and material-specific calculations remain open.

## Discovery implications

Track a controlled doping or bandwidth path with independently established magnetic, structural and superconducting observables. Distinguish tuning the filling from changing hopping, disorder or lattice geometry. Preserve the local constraints of a theoretical model and calculate gauge-invariant observables before assigning a material interpretation. A finite singlet-energy gain is a useful model check, not an experimentally verified route to high-temperature superconductivity.

## Related topics

Compare [quantum spin liquids](/scwiki/spin-liquids-and-superconductivity), [spin fluctuations](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), [superconducting gap](/scwiki/superconducting-gap) and [charge fluctuations](/scwiki/charge-fluctuation-pairing).

## Limits and disputes

Pustogow and colleagues' 2023 strain-transport study favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic candidate's 6 K anomaly. The 140 nm crystal is coupled to a PET substrate; quoted hydrostatic-equivalent pressures are inferred by comparison with transport data. The paper acknowledges that a gapped chiral spin liquid is not ruled out without a discriminating experiment. It also assigns sharp resistance jumps to mounting-related microcracks. A transport anomaly or phase-diagram shape alone must not be promoted to an unambiguous microscopic spin-state determination. [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

The Lee–Nagaosa–Wen review itself notes an experimental mismatch in the doping dependence of the Gaussian U(1) prediction for the temperature slope of superfluid density. Thus the simple response construction above has an explicit historical limitation. Naming a redundant representation U(1), SU(2) or Z2 is not sufficient to establish the corresponding emergent low-energy phase. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

Pseudogaps, Fermi arcs, singlet correlations and d-wave pairing each admit more than one theoretical description. Test a specified RVB state against physical correlation functions, charge stiffness, spectral weight, symmetry and disorder responses. Treating all these observations as interchangeable proof would remove the very distinctions needed to compare mechanisms. Full final-version, data and material-specific calculations remain open.

## Discovery implications

Track a controlled doping or bandwidth path with independently established magnetic, structural and superconducting observables. Distinguish tuning the filling from changing hopping, disorder or lattice geometry. Preserve the local constraints of a theoretical model and calculate gauge-invariant observables before assigning a material interpretation. A finite singlet-energy gain is a useful model check, not an experimentally verified route to high-temperature superconductivity.

A singlet on ordered sites $i,j$ is $|s_{ij}\rangle=(|\uparrow_i\downarrow_j\rangle-|\downarrow_i\uparrow_j\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Different products of such bonds need not be orthogonal. ### scwiki-b9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-6

A projected-electron construction writes $c_{i\sigma}=b_i^\dagger f_{i\sigma}$ with $b_i^\dagger b_i+\sum_\sigma f_{i\sigma}^\dagger f_{i\sigma}=1$. Under the internal redundancy $f_i\to e^{i\theta_i}f_i$, $b_i\to e^{i\theta_i}b_i$, the electron remains invariant. A spinon pair alone changes phase; the accompanying charge factor cancels it. articles.body:
## Scope

An isotropic, sign-preserving spin-singlet gap is the conventional s-wave reference. Three questions must nevertheless be separated: whether quasiparticles are fully gapped, how the order parameter transforms under crystal symmetry, and whether it changes sign between parts of the Fermi surface. A full gap answers the first question within the measurement's resolution; it does not settle the other two. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

For a centrosymmetric tetragonal crystal, A1g denotes the fully symmetric even-parity representation. It permits a constant gap but also higher harmonics and accidental nodes. In another crystal, use that crystal's representation labels. In multiband systems, fully open gaps can have opposite signs on different sheets; see the separate s± entry. Identifying an s-wave state also does not, by itself, identify its microscopic pairing interaction. [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

## Mathematical assumptions

The equilibrium, single-band, isotropic, constant-density-of-states weak-coupling BCS model gives $2\Delta(0)/(k_BT_c)\simeq3.528$ and $\Delta C/(\gamma T_c)\simeq1.426$, with $\gamma$ the normal electronic heat-capacity coefficient. These are limiting benchmarks, not mandatory ratios for every s-wave material. The existing independent gap and entropy checks establish these model limits; strong coupling, multiband structure and anisotropy require their own calculation. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

To illustrate symmetry without fitting a material, take a circular Fermi surface centered at the tetragonal zone center and $\Delta(\phi)=\Psi f(\phi)$, where

$$f(\phi)=1+r\cos(4\phi).$$

Rotations by $\pi/2$, reflections and inversion leave this function unchanged. For $|r|<1$ it is positive everywhere; at $|r|=1$ four zeros touch the Fermi surface without sign reversal; for $|r|>1$ there are eight sign-changing nodes. Their presence changes with a parameter rather than being required by A1g symmetry. This global fourfold example is distinct from Mishra and colleagues' local twofold harmonic on a selected off-center pocket. [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

For clean weak-coupling separable pairing with uniform angular density-of-states weight, the illustrative heat-capacity jump is

$$\frac{\Delta C}{\gamma T_c}=\frac{12}{7\zeta(3)}\frac{\langle f^2\rangle^2}{\langle f^4\rangle},\qquad \langle f^2\rangle=1+\frac{r^2}{2},\quad \langle f^4\rangle=1+3r^2+\frac{3r^4}{8}.$$

Independent angular sums and a thermal-kernel quadrature verify five cases. At $r=0.6$ the gap remains nodeless, while the jump is about $0.933$ rather than $1.426$. This shows why applying the isotropic ratio as a symmetry test can fail. It is a clean separable-model result, not a disorder simulation or a measured sample value. The cited BCS paper provides the underlying mean-field context; the angular calculation is our independent illustration. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

For a real symmetric normal Hamiltonian $h$ and an imposed uniform real gap, the block matrix $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta I\\\Delta I&-h\end{pmatrix}$ has energies $\pm\sqrt{\epsilon_n^2+\Delta^2}$. Six small-matrix checks confirm this relation with different scalar site potentials. It does not prove an unchanged self-consistent $T_c$: the normal eigenvalues, density of states and pairing matrix elements can change. Anderson's argument pairs exact time-reversed states; it is not a blanket guarantee against all chemical disorder, localization or magnetic scattering. [R2](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b)

## Experimental criteria

A magnitude-sensitive quasiparticle spectrum cannot generally determine an interband sign. Six independent-band, broadened-DOS comparisons give identical spectra after reversing one band's gap sign. This deliberately excludes interband scattering and coherent phase-sensitive tunneling. Measurements sensitive to phase or sign need their own geometry and matrix-element analysis. Low-temperature activation alone also cannot distinguish an isotropic gap from a smaller nonzero gap minimum. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

Hebel and Slichter's aluminum experiment used field cycling: nuclear spins relaxed in the superconducting state but were read out in the normal state. Its 0.94–4.2 K interval is a measurement range, not a range of transition temperatures. Nuclear relaxation tests a response with coherence effects; observing or missing a peak alone does not measure relative signs between bands. Only the original abstract has been checked here. [R4](#ref-source-99644bb2badd2d56)

Nagamatsu and colleagues' MgB2 report separates a zero-field four-probe resistance onset at 39 K from its 38 K end point, alongside magnetic measurements at 10 Oe. [R5](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b)

Choi and colleagues subsequently calculated distinct band-dependent gaps using anisotropic electron–phonon theory. The discovery experiment and the gap calculation answer different questions; neither justifies assigning one fixed gap value to every MgB2 sample. The corrected Choi DOI is nature00898. [R6](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221)

For lanthanum superhydrides, Somayazulu's sample A had room-temperature pressures of 188 GPa before and 196 GPa after cycling; pressure at the resistance change was not directly measured. The published account distinguishes four-probe data from contact-sensitive pseudo-four-probe configurations and mixed phases. Drozdov's later study reports additional field and isotope evidence, defines $T_c$ by resistance onset, and states that magnetization of its small samples remained unresolved. Neither transport report is a phase-sensitive measurement of gap sign. [R8](#ref-source-77b774e18b0f50c7) [R9](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

## Limits and disputes

Mishra and colleagues show node lifting in a model with weak pointlike scatterers treated in the Born approximation. Their single-sheet calculation can suppress $T_c$ too strongly; additional bands change that balance, while interband scattering cannot generally be discarded. This supports a conditional explanation of activated behavior after disorder, not the rule that disorder always preserves or improves s-wave superconductivity. [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

The ideal isotope value $\alpha=-d\ln T_c/d\ln M=1/2$ assumes a harmonic phonon scale and otherwise mass-independent model parameters. Sulfur-hydride isotope observations support phonon involvement within their experimental context. For lanthanum hydrides, the published methods discuss different hydride/deuteride phase mixtures and zero-point/anharmonic stability effects. Matching pressure, phase and preparation is therefore essential before interpreting a mass derivative. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R7](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434) [R9](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

## Discovery implications

Combine thermodynamics, spectroscopy, magnetic response and controlled perturbations. Keep disorder-induced carrier or structural changes separate from elastic scattering, and distinguish small gaps from true nodes within a stated temperature window. Track superconducting evidence, symmetry, relative phase and pairing interaction as separate conclusions. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R2](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b) [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9) [R9](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

## Related topics

Read [BCS theory](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), [Eliashberg theory](/scwiki/eliashberg-strong-coupling), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [energy gaps](/scwiki/superconducting-gap).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-c1-claim-scope-1

An isotropic, sign-preserving spin-singlet gap is the conventional s-wave reference. Three questions must nevertheless be separated: whether quasiparticles are fully gapped, how the order parameter transforms under crystal symmetry, and whether it changes sign between parts of the Fermi surface. A full gap answers the first question within the measurement's resolution; it does not settle the other two.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-ba10e800a1246bf6, source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9.

Conditions: Separate symmetry, magnitude, relative phase and interaction. Toy models assume declared circular Fermi surface, separable pairing, imposed gap or independent bands; not material fits.

### scwiki-c1-claim-scope-2

For a centrosymmetric tetragonal crystal, A1g denotes the fully symmetric even-parity representation. It permits a constant gap but also higher harmonics and accidental nodes. In another crystal, use that crystal's representation labels. In multiband systems, fully open gaps can have opposite signs on different sheets; see the separate s± entry. Identifying an s-wave state also does not, by itself, identify its microscopic pairing interaction.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9.

Conditions: Separate symmetry, magnitude, relative phase and interaction. Toy models assume declared circular Fermi surface, separable pairing, imposed gap or independent bands; not material fits.

These are limiting benchmarks, not mandatory ratios for every s-wave material. The existing independent gap and entropy checks establish these model limits; strong coupling, multiband structure and anisotropy require their own calculation.

Independent angular sums and a thermal-kernel quadrature verify five cases. At $r=0.6$ the gap remains nodeless, while the jump is about $0.933$ rather than $1.426$. This shows why applying the isotropic ratio as a symmetry test can fail. It is a clean separable-model result, not a disorder simulation or a measured sample value. ### scwiki-c1-claim-mathematical-assumptions-8

For a real symmetric normal Hamiltonian $h$ and an imposed uniform real gap, the block matrix $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta I\\\Delta I&-h\end{pmatrix}$ has energies $\pm\sqrt{\epsilon_n^2+\Delta^2}$. Six small-matrix checks confirm this relation with different scalar site potentials. It does not prove an unchanged self-consistent $T_c$: the normal eigenvalues, density of states and pairing matrix elements can change. Anderson's argument pairs exact time-reversed states; it is not a blanket guarantee against all chemical disorder, localization or magnetic scattering.

### scwiki-c1-claim-experimental-criteria-1

A magnitude-sensitive quasiparticle spectrum cannot generally determine an interband sign. Six independent-band, broadened-DOS comparisons give identical spectra after reversing one band's gap sign. This deliberately excludes interband scattering and coherent phase-sensitive tunneling. Measurements sensitive to phase or sign need their own geometry and matrix-element analysis. Low-temperature activation alone also cannot distinguish an isotropic gap from a smaller nonzero gap minimum.

### scwiki-c1-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Mishra and colleagues show node lifting in a model with weak pointlike scatterers treated in the Born approximation. Their single-sheet calculation can suppress $T_c$ too strongly; additional bands change that balance, while interband scattering cannot generally be discarded. This supports a conditional explanation of activated behavior after disorder, not the rule that disorder always preserves or improves s-wave superconductivity.

### scwiki-c1-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

The ideal isotope value $\alpha=-d\ln T_c/d\ln M=1/2$ assumes a harmonic phonon scale and otherwise mass-independent model parameters. Sulfur-hydride isotope observations support phonon involvement within their experimental context. For lanthanum hydrides, the published methods discuss different hydride/deuteride phase mixtures and zero-point/anharmonic stability effects. Matching pressure, phase and preparation is therefore essential before interpreting a mass derivative.

Combine thermodynamics, spectroscopy, magnetic response and controlled perturbations. Keep disorder-induced carrier or structural changes separate from elastic scattering, and distinguish small gaps from true nodes within a stated temperature window. articles.body:
## Scope

The label s± describes a superconducting gap whose sign differs between relevant Fermi-surface sheets. In common iron-based models the state belongs to the fully symmetric A1g representation, while different pockets carry opposite gap signs. A fully open gap therefore does not establish a sign-preserving state. The precise pocket and orbital assignments must come from the actual material rather than a generic two-pocket drawing. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

## Mathematical assumptions

A minimal illustration is

$
\Delta_h=+\Delta_1,\qquad
\Delta_e=-\Delta_2.
$

The labels $h$ and $e$ refer to hole and electron pockets in the model, not to a universal inventory present in every iron-based superconductor. Repulsive interband scattering can favor opposite signs in a linearized pairing equation. Mazin and colleagues and Kuroki and colleagues developed important iron-based proposals, but their predictions depend on the Fermi surface and interaction assumptions. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

An A1g gap can also be anisotropic and can develop accidental nodes. This possibility should be distinguished from symmetry-enforced nodes in another representation. ## Corrected nodal example

Reid and colleagues' 2012 thermal-conductivity paper, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.087001, is about KFe2As2. The authors report residual heat transport consistent with nodes and argue for a d-wave interpretation. It is not a P-substituted Ba122 paper. The previous attribution is corrected in the source mapping and in the register for C2 and C10. No replacement P-Ba122 claim is silently inferred from this DOI. [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

## Limits and disputes

FeSe, shallow-band systems, strongly hole-doped endpoints and electron-only interfaces can require models different from the original hole-electron-pocket proposal. A candidate s± solution for a nickelate is a theoretical proposal until an appropriate experiment constrains it. Gap magnitude, gap sign, nodes and the microscopic pairing interaction are separate inference steps. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

## Discovery implications

Specify which sheets are expected to change sign and what observation could reject that assignment. Use measured electronic structure, compare several independent probes and retain sample composition. For agent retrieval, quote the claim together with the named material and source; the sign structure is not an unconditional property of the phrase “iron-based superconductor.” [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R4](#ref-source-3ee65ce8fc5080da) [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

claims.statement: For the tetragonal point group D4h, the familiar $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state belongs to B1g: a quarter turn changes its sign, while inversion preserves it. This entry separates symmetry, low-energy excitations and phase-sensitive evidence. A node or a small gap alone does not identify B1g, and identifying B1g does not uniquely determine the interaction that produced pairing. The cuprate evidence combines complementary measurements rather than a single universal diagnostic.

articles.body:
## Scope

For the tetragonal point group D4h, the familiar $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state belongs to B1g: a quarter turn changes its sign, while inversion preserves it. This entry separates symmetry, low-energy excitations and phase-sensitive evidence. A node or a small gap alone does not identify B1g, and identifying B1g does not uniquely determine the interaction that produced pairing. The cuprate evidence combines complementary measurements rather than a single universal diagnostic. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

The usual even-parity spin-singlet description assumes a centrosymmetric setting with the appropriate spin or pseudospin pairing structure. Orthorhombicity, multiple bands and additional broken symmetries require the actual crystal symmetry to be used. A label inherited from an ideal square lattice is not a substitute for that analysis. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

## Mathematical assumptions

An illustrative lattice harmonic, with lattice spacing set to one, is $\Delta(\mathbf k)=\Delta_0[\cos k_x-\cos k_y]/2$. Direct rotation, diagonal-reflection and inversion checks establish its B1g transformation. Its diagonal zero lines produce quasiparticle nodes only where they intersect the Fermi surface. A circular contour centered at the zone center intersects them; hypothetical small pockets around $(\pi,0)$ and $(0,\pi)$ do not. The latter have opposite gap signs while each pocket remains fully gapped. These checks establish a geometric possibility, not a band structure for a particular cuprate. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

On a circular Fermi surface, $f(\phi)=\cos2\phi$ has four zeros. A real admixture $f=\cos2\phi+s$ shifts the four nodes for $|s|<1$, gives two touching zeros at $|s|=1$, and removes them for $|s|>1$. Such a mixture is not pure B1g in a tetragonal crystal; orthorhombic symmetry can permit the corresponding real components to mix. The complex illustrative mixture $\cos2\phi+is$ instead has minimum magnitude $|s|$ and, when both components are nonzero, breaks time reversal. Five direct checks distinguish these cases. They do not demonstrate that any material selects the mixture. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

Near one simple node, take $E(\mathbf q)=\sqrt{(v_Fq_1)^2+(v_\Delta q_2)^2}$ in units $\hbar=k_B=1$. The ellipse of states below $E$ has area $\pi E^2/(v_Fv_\Delta)$; dividing by $(2\pi)^2$ and differentiating gives a positive-energy density of states $g(E)=E/(2\pi v_Fv_\Delta)$ for this one declared branch. Polygon-area checks verify six cases. For a linear density $g(E)=aE$, a converged thermal integral gives $C=(9\zeta(3)/2)aT^2$. Spin, node and band multiplicities must be supplied consistently. This clean local model illustrates a power law; disorder, finite temperature windows and different nodal dispersions change its applicability. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

For a separate illustration of phase frustration, consider a zero-field, single-junction loop with a built-in $\pi$ phase shift. Writing $f=\Phi/\Phi_0$, $\Phi_0=h/(2e)$ and $\beta=2\pi LI_c/\Phi_0$, with $E_J=\Phi_0 I_c/(2\pi)$, its energy is $U/E_J=2\pi^2f^2/\beta+\cos(2\pi f)$. The stationary condition is $f=\beta\sin(2\pi f)/(2\pi)$. Five energy-minimization checks show a zero-flux minimum for $\beta\leq1$ and paired nonzero minima for $\beta>1$; their magnitude approaches one half only as the inductance parameter grows. A finite loop therefore need not contain exactly half a flux quantum. This is not a reproduction of the extended three-boundary tricrystal geometry used in the experiments below. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

## Experimental criteria

Hardy and colleagues measured changes in penetration depth in YBa2Cu3O6.95 using a 900 MHz resonator. Their abstract reports a linear contribution over approximately 3–25 K, within measurements extending from 1.3 K to the transition. This supports low-energy nodal excitations; the temperature interval is not a reported transition-temperature interval. Only the publisher abstract is checked here, so the full calibration, defect comparison and raw traces remain outside this review. [R2](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

Shen and colleagues' 1993 Bi2212 photoemission report finds a large in-plane gap anisotropy compatible with $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Photoemission primarily constrains excitation energies and gap magnitude; it does not directly read the relative order-parameter phase. The pinned chapter's DOI ending in 75.4234 actually identifies a Brillouin-spectroscopy paper and is corrected to 70.1553. Published comments and replies in 1993 and 1994 have been identified but not fully examined; the early ARPES result is not presented as a standalone final symmetry proof. [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

The original 1994 tricrystal-ring and 1995 scanning-SQUID papers are retained as historical source pointers. Their identities are checked, but this entry's detailed geometry discussion relies on the explicitly reviewed later author manuscripts, rather than claiming a new full audit of those originals. [R4](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R5](#ref-source-6fe9eb9d2301fe93)

In the 2004 study of Ca-doped Y-123, La-214 and Bi-2212 films, selected crystal orientations create an odd phase frustration for a predominantly $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state. The authors compare opposite vortex polarities and model the pickup-loop response. The La-214 fit allowing flux to vary gives $0.585\pm0.1\,\Phi_0$, compatible with one half within its stated uncertainty. Imaging at 4.2 K is distinct from the samples' transition temperatures. Constraints on a fixed imaginary component depend on resolution; sufficiently small alternating domains are an explicitly discussed caveat. Doping coordinates are estimated using an empirical relation, and grain-boundary doping need not exactly equal bulk doping. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

The 2000 electron-doped study tests NCCO and PCCO films. For NCCO it compares a frustrated tricrystal with two unfrustrated geometries; the controls show little central flux. Sensor height and pickup-loop integration enter the field model. Allowing total flux to vary gives $0.47^{+0.18}_{-0.14}\,\Phi_0$ in the quoted NCCO fit; the authors define the uncertainty using a doubling of best-fit chi-square, not an asserted standard confidence interval. This is sample- and geometry-specific phase evidence. The reported 22–25 K NCCO and 22–23 K PCCO transition ranges are separate from 4.2 K imaging and junction measurements; no single transition criterion is invented for the material table. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Low-temperature power laws, gap anisotropy and phase-sensitive interference probe different quantities. Interpret them with sample composition, disorder, field, temperature range, surface sensitivity and interface geometry attached. A magnitude-only spectrum cannot distinguish a gap from another function with the same absolute value; this mathematical ambiguity does not imply that every such function is a smooth, physically realizable pairing state. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

Spin-fluctuation calculations provide one route to a sign-changing gap, subject to their input spectrum and approximations. Their agreement with a symmetry assignment does not prove a unique pairing mechanism. High transition temperatures or family membership likewise cannot replace a phase-sensitive measurement of a particular pressure state. [R8](#ref-source-7755cb2d156620a8)

The 2019 oxygen-17 NMR work on Sr2RuO4 constrains earlier order-parameter proposals by observing a Knight-shift reduction. This does not automatically establish B1g pairing. The inherited review distinguishes RF heating, strain and applied-field conditions; a complete current order-parameter survey remains separate work. [R9](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41)

## Discovery implications

For a candidate material, first state its point group and measured Fermi surface. Then ask which experiments constrain node locations, spin response and relative phase, and whether those measurements describe comparable sample states. A useful next experiment should distinguish competing explanations within a specified geometry and resolution. Keep computed pairing preference, observed superconductivity and experimentally constrained symmetry as separate conclusions. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826) [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Related topics

Read [s-wave symmetry](/scwiki/s-wave), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [spin-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), and [superconducting gaps](/scwiki/superconducting-gap).

On a circular Fermi surface, $f(\phi)=\cos2\phi$ has four zeros. A real admixture $f=\cos2\phi+s$ shifts the four nodes for $|s|<1$, gives two touching zeros at $|s|=1$, and removes them for $|s|>1$. Such a mixture is not pure B1g in a tetragonal crystal; orthorhombic symmetry can permit the corresponding real components to mix. The complex illustrative mixture $\cos2\phi+is$ instead has minimum magnitude $|s|$ and, when both components are nonzero, breaks time reversal. Five direct checks distinguish these cases. They do not demonstrate that any material selects the mixture. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

Near one simple node, take $E(\mathbf q)=\sqrt{(v_Fq_1)^2+(v_\Delta q_2)^2}$ in units $\hbar=k_B=1$. The ellipse of states below $E$ has area $\pi E^2/(v_Fv_\Delta)$; dividing by $(2\pi)^2$ and differentiating gives a positive-energy density of states $g(E)=E/(2\pi v_Fv_\Delta)$ for this one declared branch. Polygon-area checks verify six cases. For a linear density $g(E)=aE$, a converged thermal integral gives $C=(9\zeta(3)/2)aT^2$. Spin, node and band multiplicities must be supplied consistently. This clean local model illustrates a power law; disorder, finite temperature windows and different nodal dispersions change its applicability. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

For a separate illustration of phase frustration, consider a zero-field, single-junction loop with a built-in $\pi$ phase shift. Writing $f=\Phi/\Phi_0$, $\Phi_0=h/(2e)$ and $\beta=2\pi LI_c/\Phi_0$, with $E_J=\Phi_0 I_c/(2\pi)$, its energy is $U/E_J=2\pi^2f^2/\beta+\cos(2\pi f)$. The stationary condition is $f=\beta\sin(2\pi f)/(2\pi)$. Five energy-minimization checks show a zero-flux minimum for $\beta\leq1$ and paired nonzero minima for $\beta>1$; their magnitude approaches one half only as the inductance parameter grows. A finite loop therefore need not contain exactly half a flux quantum. This is not a reproduction of the extended three-boundary tricrystal geometry used in the experiments below. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

## Experimental criteria

Hardy and colleagues measured changes in penetration depth in YBa2Cu3O6.95 using a 900 MHz resonator. Their abstract reports a linear contribution over approximately 3–25 K, within measurements extending from 1.3 K to the transition. This supports low-energy nodal excitations; the temperature interval is not a reported transition-temperature interval. Only the publisher abstract is checked here, so the full calibration, defect comparison and raw traces remain outside this review. [R2](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

Shen and colleagues' 1993 Bi2212 photoemission report finds a large in-plane gap anisotropy compatible with $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Photoemission primarily constrains excitation energies and gap magnitude; it does not directly read the relative order-parameter phase. The pinned chapter's DOI ending in 75.4234 actually identifies a Brillouin-spectroscopy paper and is corrected to 70.1553. Published comments and replies in 1993 and 1994 have been identified but not fully examined; the early ARPES result is not presented as a standalone final symmetry proof. [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

The original 1994 tricrystal-ring and 1995 scanning-SQUID papers are retained as historical source pointers. Their identities are checked, but this entry's detailed geometry discussion relies on the explicitly reviewed later author manuscripts, rather than claiming a new full audit of those originals. [R4](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R5](#ref-source-6fe9eb9d2301fe93)

In the 2004 study of Ca-doped Y-123, La-214 and Bi-2212 films, selected crystal orientations create an odd phase frustration for a predominantly $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state. The authors compare opposite vortex polarities and model the pickup-loop response. The La-214 fit allowing flux to vary gives $0.585\pm0.1\,\Phi_0$, compatible with one half within its stated uncertainty. Imaging at 4.2 K is distinct from the samples' transition temperatures. Constraints on a fixed imaginary component depend on resolution; sufficiently small alternating domains are an explicitly discussed caveat. Doping coordinates are estimated using an empirical relation, and grain-boundary doping need not exactly equal bulk doping. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

The 2000 electron-doped study tests NCCO and PCCO films. For NCCO it compares a frustrated tricrystal with two unfrustrated geometries; the controls show little central flux. Sensor height and pickup-loop integration enter the field model. Allowing total flux to vary gives $0.47^{+0.18}_{-0.14}\,\Phi_0$ in the quoted NCCO fit; the authors define the uncertainty using a doubling of best-fit chi-square, not an asserted standard confidence interval. This is sample- and geometry-specific phase evidence. The reported 22–25 K NCCO and 22–23 K PCCO transition ranges are separate from 4.2 K imaging and junction measurements; no single transition criterion is invented for the material table. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Low-temperature power laws, gap anisotropy and phase-sensitive interference probe different quantities. Interpret them with sample composition, disorder, field, temperature range, surface sensitivity and interface geometry attached. A magnitude-only spectrum cannot distinguish a gap from another function with the same absolute value; this mathematical ambiguity does not imply that every such function is a smooth, physically realizable pairing state. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

Spin-fluctuation calculations provide one route to a sign-changing gap, subject to their input spectrum and approximations. Their agreement with a symmetry assignment does not prove a unique pairing mechanism. High transition temperatures or family membership likewise cannot replace a phase-sensitive measurement of a particular pressure state. [R8](#ref-source-7755cb2d156620a8)

The 2019 oxygen-17 NMR work on Sr2RuO4 constrains earlier order-parameter proposals by observing a Knight-shift reduction. This does not automatically establish B1g pairing. The inherited review distinguishes RF heating, strain and applied-field conditions; a complete current order-parameter survey remains separate work. [R9](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41)

## Discovery implications

For a candidate material, first state its point group and measured Fermi surface. Then ask which experiments constrain node locations, spin response and relative phase, and whether those measurements describe comparable sample states. A useful next experiment should distinguish competing explanations within a specified geometry and resolution. Keep computed pairing preference, observed superconductivity and experimentally constrained symmetry as separate conclusions. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826) [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

claims.statement: In a tetragonal D4h crystal, a single-component $d_{xy}$ gap transforms as B2g. It is distinct from the B1g $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state when both are described using the same crystallographic axes. Both are even under inversion; the usual spin-singlet interpretation assumes the corresponding centrosymmetric spin or pseudospin setting. This entry covers symmetry and tests of a B2g candidate, not a claim that every material with line nodes realizes it.

articles.body:
## Scope

In a tetragonal D4h crystal, a single-component $d_{xy}$ gap transforms as B2g. It is distinct from the B1g $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state when both are described using the same crystallographic axes. Both are even under inversion; the usual spin-singlet interpretation assumes the corresponding centrosymmetric spin or pseudospin setting. This entry covers symmetry and tests of a B2g candidate, not a claim that every material with line nodes realizes it. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

No sample in this entry is classified as experimentally established B2g. This describes the present review's evidence, not a proof that no such material exists. A calculated pairing channel, an Fe dxy orbital contribution and an experimentally determined gap representation are three different statements. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

## Mathematical assumptions

With lattice spacing one, an illustrative harmonic is $\Delta(\mathbf k)=\Delta_0\sin k_x\sin k_y$. It changes sign under either axial reflection and under a quarter turn, but is unchanged by inversion or interchange of $k_x$ and $k_y$. These transformations give B2g for the stated axes. Gap zeros lie on axial lines, including their periodic zone-boundary counterparts; quasiparticle nodes require intersections with the Fermi surface. Higher harmonics can add zeros without changing the representation. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

Coordinate conventions matter. For a unit circular contour, $2xy=\sin2\phi$ and $x^2-y^2=\cos2\phi$. Under the passive coordinate change $x'=(x+y)/\sqrt2$, $y'=(-x+y)/\sqrt2$, one finds $x'^2-y'^2=2xy$. The polynomial name changes while the physical pattern relative to the crystal is unchanged. Four direct checks verify this identity. A comparison between Fe–Fe and Fe–As coordinate conventions must therefore include the axes and symmetry operations, rather than matching the word “d-wave” alone. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

On an ideal circular contour with uniform weight, replacing $\cos2\phi$ by $\sin2\phi$ is an angular shift. Four independent broadened-density-of-states integrals coincide for the two gaps; both also have $\langle f^2\rangle=1/2$ and $\langle f^4\rangle=3/8$. Consequently an angularly averaged spectrum or a clean nodal power law can fail to distinguish these orientations. The checks assume identical amplitudes and broadening. Real velocity weights, multiple sheets and selective probes can break this equivalence. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

To isolate what a pairing eigenvalue does, define normalized basis functions $u_s=1$, $u_1=\sqrt2\cos2\phi$, $u_2=\sqrt2\sin2\phi$ and a deliberately separable operator $K(\phi,\phi')=\sum_a\lambda_a u_a(\phi)u_a(\phi')$, integrated with $d\phi'/(2\pi)$. Numerical application confirms the prescribed eigenvalues for three choices: $(0.3,0.4,0.1)$ selects B1g, $(0.3,0.2,0.45)$ selects B2g, and $(0.3,0.4,0.4)$ makes the two d channels degenerate. These couplings were chosen, not inferred from a material. The equality is accidental within this example: D4h does not require its two distinct one-dimensional representations to have equal pairing strength. The calculation illustrates model selection, not an RPA reproduction or a measured transition temperature. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

An orbital basis change must act on both electrons of a pair: $\Delta_{\rm band}(\mathbf k)=U^\dagger(\mathbf k)\Delta_{\rm orbital}(\mathbf k)U^*(-\mathbf k)$. Four real, momentum-independent two-orbital examples change matrix entries while preserving the imposed gap-matrix eigenvalues. This limited check does not replace the full momentum-dependent transformation. Likewise, two electrons in the same dxy orbital contribute the product of the orbital's symmetry characters; an orbital sign squared is positive. The orbital name alone therefore does not assign a B2g momentum dependence to the pair. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

## Experimental criteria

Momentum-resolved measurements must locate a gap minimum or node relative to measured crystal axes and Fermi sheets. Distinguish insufficient energy resolution from a true zero and compare temperatures within the same superconducting state. Thermodynamic power laws can motivate a nodal hypothesis, but without directional information they do not distinguish B1g from B2g in the circular example above. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Rotating-field measurements also require a response model. Vorontsov and Vekhter calculate a reversal of specific-heat anisotropy with temperature or field while the imposed nodal directions remain fixed. Their quasiclassical treatment includes vortex scattering, a corrugated quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface and impurity scattering; the selected manuscript neglects Zeeman splitting. The authors caution that their spatial-averaging approximation can overestimate vortex scattering at low fields. Thus a heat-capacity minimum is not universally a node locator. Their comparison with CeCoIn5 favors B1g within that analysis; this is not evidence establishing B2g. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

The thermal weighting itself can be checked without reproducing that calculation. In units $k_B=1$, the factor $w(x)=x^2e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})^2$, with $x=E/T$, peaks near $2.399$. For a deliberately chosen bounded spectral difference $\delta N(E)=0.1[1-(E/E_*)^2]e^{-(E/E_*)^2}$, five converged integrals of $w(x)\delta N(Tx)$ change sign as temperature increases. The total spectra can remain positive by adding this small difference to a unit background. This illustrates finite-energy weighting; it does not calculate vortices, assign a physical inversion temperature or validate a material symmetry. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

Phase-sensitive junction tests need a geometry that distinguishes the candidate representations, with calibrated crystal orientations and controls for trapped flux and interfaces. The reviewed electron-doped cuprate tricrystal experiment demonstrates why frustrated and unfrustrated control geometries matter. Its result concerns those samples and the tested $d_{x^2-y^2}$ pattern; it cannot simply be relabeled as a dxy measurement. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Graser and colleagues explicitly align their orbital basis with nearest-neighbor Fe–Fe directions. In their five-orbital model, the principal competition discussed is anisotropic s-wave versus $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Equation (33) separately defines dxy by its reflection characters, and Figure 13 includes it as a subleading channel for the displayed electron-doped, zero-Hund-coupling case. That calculated ordering depends on parameters; it neither establishes a B2g material nor justifies reading an orbital-weight plot as a gap-symmetry plot. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

Bickers, Scalapino and White provide an early conserving-approximation framework for the two-dimensional Hubbard model. The abstract checked here does not establish a B2g-specific result. Kuroki and colleagues' later five-orbital work must be read with its 2009 erratum: an orbital-to-band transformation error changed the original gap plot. The corrected displayed diagonal band gaps are fully open, while parameter-dependent nodal competition remains. This correction is retained as a required companion citation. [R3](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0) [R4](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

A complex combination of two d components is a separate state, not the single-component B2g case covered here. Likewise, changing to an orthorhombic or hexagonal crystal requires a new symmetry classification. Do not assume that a familiar polynomial name carries the same representation, enforced zeros or degeneracy into a different point group. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

## Discovery implications

For a proposed dxy candidate, specify the crystal axes, point group, band or orbital basis, and the sample state. Compare competing representations using both directional and phase information, with temperature, field and interface assumptions attached. Keep the present absence of an accepted material record separate from the existence of a theoretical channel. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462) [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Related topics

Read [d-wave phase evidence](/scwiki/d-wave), [s-wave symmetry](/scwiki/s-wave), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [spin-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), and [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing).

A comparison between Fe–Fe and Fe–As coordinate conventions must therefore include the axes and symmetry operations, rather than matching the word “d-wave” alone. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

On an ideal circular contour with uniform weight, replacing $\cos2\phi$ by $\sin2\phi$ is an angular shift. Four independent broadened-density-of-states integrals coincide for the two gaps; both also have $\langle f^2\rangle=1/2$ and $\langle f^4\rangle=3/8$. Consequently an angularly averaged spectrum or a clean nodal power law can fail to distinguish these orientations. The checks assume identical amplitudes and broadening. Real velocity weights, multiple sheets and selective probes can break this equivalence. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

To isolate what a pairing eigenvalue does, define normalized basis functions $u_s=1$, $u_1=\sqrt2\cos2\phi$, $u_2=\sqrt2\sin2\phi$ and a deliberately separable operator $K(\phi,\phi')=\sum_a\lambda_a u_a(\phi)u_a(\phi')$, integrated with $d\phi'/(2\pi)$. Numerical application confirms the prescribed eigenvalues for three choices: $(0.3,0.4,0.1)$ selects B1g, $(0.3,0.2,0.45)$ selects B2g, and $(0.3,0.4,0.4)$ makes the two d channels degenerate. These couplings were chosen, not inferred from a material. The equality is accidental within this example: D4h does not require its two distinct one-dimensional representations to have equal pairing strength. The calculation illustrates model selection, not an RPA reproduction or a measured transition temperature. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

An orbital basis change must act on both electrons of a pair: $\Delta_{\rm band}(\mathbf k)=U^\dagger(\mathbf k)\Delta_{\rm orbital}(\mathbf k)U^*(-\mathbf k)$. Four real, momentum-independent two-orbital examples change matrix entries while preserving the imposed gap-matrix eigenvalues. This limited check does not replace the full momentum-dependent transformation. Likewise, two electrons in the same dxy orbital contribute the product of the orbital's symmetry characters; an orbital sign squared is positive. The orbital name alone therefore does not assign a B2g momentum dependence to the pair. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

## Experimental criteria

Momentum-resolved measurements must locate a gap minimum or node relative to measured crystal axes and Fermi sheets. Distinguish insufficient energy resolution from a true zero and compare temperatures within the same superconducting state. Thermodynamic power laws can motivate a nodal hypothesis, but without directional information they do not distinguish B1g from B2g in the circular example above. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Rotating-field measurements also require a response model. Vorontsov and Vekhter calculate a reversal of specific-heat anisotropy with temperature or field while the imposed nodal directions remain fixed. Their quasiclassical treatment includes vortex scattering, a corrugated quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface and impurity scattering; the selected manuscript neglects Zeeman splitting. The authors caution that their spatial-averaging approximation can overestimate vortex scattering at low fields. Thus a heat-capacity minimum is not universally a node locator. Their comparison with CeCoIn5 favors B1g within that analysis; this is not evidence establishing B2g. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

The thermal weighting itself can be checked without reproducing that calculation. In units $k_B=1$, the factor $w(x)=x^2e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})^2$, with $x=E/T$, peaks near $2.399$. For a deliberately chosen bounded spectral difference $\delta N(E)=0.1[1-(E/E_*)^2]e^{-(E/E_*)^2}$, five converged integrals of $w(x)\delta N(Tx)$ change sign as temperature increases. The total spectra can remain positive by adding this small difference to a unit background. This illustrates finite-energy weighting; it does not calculate vortices, assign a physical inversion temperature or validate a material symmetry. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

Phase-sensitive junction tests need a geometry that distinguishes the candidate representations, with calibrated crystal orientations and controls for trapped flux and interfaces. The reviewed electron-doped cuprate tricrystal experiment demonstrates why frustrated and unfrustrated control geometries matter. Its result concerns those samples and the tested $d_{x^2-y^2}$ pattern; it cannot simply be relabeled as a dxy measurement. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Graser and colleagues explicitly align their orbital basis with nearest-neighbor Fe–Fe directions. In their five-orbital model, the principal competition discussed is anisotropic s-wave versus $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Equation (33) separately defines dxy by its reflection characters, and Figure 13 includes it as a subleading channel for the displayed electron-doped, zero-Hund-coupling case. That calculated ordering depends on parameters; it neither establishes a B2g material nor justifies reading an orbital-weight plot as a gap-symmetry plot. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

Bickers, Scalapino and White provide an early conserving-approximation framework for the two-dimensional Hubbard model. The abstract checked here does not establish a B2g-specific result. Kuroki and colleagues' later five-orbital work must be read with its 2009 erratum: an orbital-to-band transformation error changed the original gap plot. The corrected displayed diagonal band gaps are fully open, while parameter-dependent nodal competition remains. This correction is retained as a required companion citation. [R3](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0) [R4](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

A complex combination of two d components is a separate state, not the single-component B2g case covered here. Likewise, changing to an orthorhombic or hexagonal crystal requires a new symmetry classification. Do not assume that a familiar polynomial name carries the same representation, enforced zeros or degeneracy into a different point group. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

## Discovery implications

For a proposed dxy candidate, specify the crystal axes, point group, band or orbital basis, and the sample state. Compare competing representations using both directional and phase information, with temperature, field and interface assumptions attached. Keep the present absence of an accepted material record separate from the existence of a theoretical channel. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. ## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-c4-claim-scope-1

In a tetragonal D4h crystal, a single-component $d_{xy}$ gap transforms as B2g. It is distinct from the B1g $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state when both are described using the same crystallographic axes. Both are even under inversion; the usual spin-singlet interpretation assumes the corresponding centrosymmetric spin or pseudospin setting. This entry covers symmetry and tests of a B2g candidate, not a claim that every material with line nodes realizes it.

### scwiki-c4-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

With lattice spacing one, an illustrative harmonic is $\Delta(\mathbf k)=\Delta_0\sin k_x\sin k_y$. Gap zeros lie on axial lines, including their periodic zone-boundary counterparts; quasiparticle nodes require intersections with the Fermi surface. Higher harmonics can add zeros without changing the representation.

articles.body:
## Scope

Two-dimensional geometry and interface location are different coordinates. A film can have weak out-of-plane electronic dispersion without displaying a clean two-dimensional phase transition. An interface can host a superconducting region even when its two constituents are not superconducting alone. Neither statement identifies one universal mechanism for increasing a critical temperature. [R1](#ref-source-ea5d0c80335c450d) [R2](#ref-source-684b96e9dbb65a64)

An interface may change charge transfer, oxygen defects, strain, orbital structure, phonons and disorder at the same time. Pair formation and macroscopic phase coherence can also occur at different scales. A useful report states whether a temperature comes from a spectral gap, resistive onset, zero resistance, magnetic screening or a BKT analysis. [R4](#ref-source-a95bcf0cb2681557) [R5](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc) [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Mathematical assumptions

For an ideal two-dimensional phase model, the BKT universal jump can be written in an energy-stiffness convention as

$
k_BT_{\mathrm{BKT}}=\frac{\pi}{2}J_s(T_{\mathrm{BKT}}^-).
$

Here $J_s$ is the renormalized total phase stiffness immediately below the transition. The normalization and the relevant long-wavelength limit must be stated. The relation does not apply directly to a bare mean-field pairing amplitude, and it does not separately measure a geometric contribution to the total stiffness. Finite size, inhomogeneity and interlayer coupling can modify an experimental comparison. [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

BCS-like amplitude formation and BKT-like phase ordering describe different aspects of a system. Treating them as mutually exclusive microscopic pairing mechanisms would confuse an interaction model with a phase-coherence transition. [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Experimental criteria

Combine independent phase-sensitive observables rather than fitting one resistive tail. Test non-linear current-voltage behavior, a suitable fluctuation-transport regime and sheet stiffness where available. Check finite-size effects, heating, current range and measurement frequency. A large anisotropy of the upper critical field is not by itself a BKT proof.

At LaAlO3/SrTiO3, Reyren and colleagues reported an interface transition around 200 mK with two-dimensional behavior. The source's inferred superconducting thickness is an upper bound, not an exact directly imaged electronic width. Gating can tune an interface phase diagram without proving that carrier density is its only control parameter. [R1](#ref-source-ea5d0c80335c450d)

## Interface examples

Cuprate heterostructures constructed from non-superconducting components demonstrate that an interface can support superconductivity. Gozar and colleagues and the layer-selective work of Logvenov and colleagues constrain where the superconducting response occurs. They establish particular interface states rather than the claim that interlayer coupling is irrelevant to every high-temperature cuprate. [R2](#ref-source-684b96e9dbb65a64) [R3](#ref-source-7fcd7faadf66481b)

For single-layer FeSe/SrTiO3, a roughly 65 ± 5 K ARPES pairing scale retains its spectroscopic label. Replica-band evidence supports an interface electron-phonon interaction, but does not quantify every contribution to the full pairing kernel. This number cannot satisfy a query requiring zero resistance, even though it is a valid temperature observation. [R4](#ref-source-a95bcf0cb2681557) [R5](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc)

## Limits and disputes

A dome-shaped gate dependence does not uniquely identify a quantum critical pairing interaction. Ionic gating also needs electrochemical controls. A superconducting single layer shows that one layer can suffice under the reported conditions, not that dimensionality or interlayer coupling never matters. Interface improvements should not be merged with bulk or transient temperature records. [R1](#ref-source-ea5d0c80335c450d) [R3](#ref-source-7fcd7faadf66481b) [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Discovery implications

Plan controls that separate thickness, interface termination, oxygen, strain and electrostatics. Report sample-to-sample variation alongside the most favorable device. A mechanism becomes more useful when it predicts which independent interface modification should change a gap scale and which should change phase stiffness. Keep those two outcomes separate in both the narrative and structured evidence. [R5](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc) [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Related topics

See [transport evidence](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [geometric stiffness](/scwiki/geometric-superfluid-weight).

articles.body:
## Scope

Cuprates share CuO2 planes as a central electronic motif, but they do not share one complete phase diagram. Layer count, apical oxygen, charge-reservoir blocks, disorder and the sign and amount of doping vary across families. The La-Ba-Cu-O discovery and the subsequent Y-Ba-Cu-O work established the high-temperature cuprate research platform; they do not make every later composition equivalent. [R1](#ref-source-ad4ee05105f93caf) [R2](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e)

Many parent compounds are antiferromagnetic correlated insulators. Doping can produce superconductivity together with pseudogap behavior, charge correlations and unusual normal-state transport. A schematic dome is an organizing picture rather than a universal quantitative equation for all compounds. A weak-coupling phonon-only explanation is not a complete account of the family, while Cooper pairing and broken-symmetry descriptions remain useful. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

## Mathematical assumptions

A frequently used illustrative form of a two-dimensional d-wave gap is

$
\Delta(\mathbf k)\propto\cos k_x-\cos k_y.
$

This lattice expression represents a symmetry structure in an appropriate square-lattice description. It is not a fit to every Fermi surface, and it does not specify a pairing mediator or an absolute gap magnitude. The significance of a sign change must be connected to phase-sensitive and momentum-resolved evidence in the named material. [R5](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

## Experimental criteria

Keep a transport onset, zero-resistance point, magnetic response and thermodynamic anomaly in separate fields. Record pressure, medium, oxygen content, preparation route and sample form. For a gap-symmetry claim, combine phase-sensitive tests with complementary spectroscopy and low-energy response. Tricrystal experiments provide an important phase-sensitive cuprate constraint; their interpretation should not be extended automatically to every electron-doped, highly disordered or pressure-treated sample. [R5](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7)

The familiar Hg-1223 examples illustrate the danger of unconditioned comparisons: the historical ambient-pressure transition near 133 K and a high-pressure scale near 164 K around 31 GPa concern different conditions. The pilot leaves an individual onset-versus-zero criterion unknown where this scoped review has not re-extracted it. That missing field must not be silently supplied by a search or an agent. [R3](#ref-source-d95477ebe515f481) [R4](#ref-source-6d09a24a26a15997)

## Limits and disputes

Antiferromagnetic correlations, a pseudogap and charge order constrain a microscopic theory without selecting one unique pairing glue. A charge-density modulation is not by itself evidence of a pair-density wave. Likewise, a linear-temperature resistivity is not an automatic measurement of a Planckian scattering time. The observable and the inference must remain separate. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

The source chapter includes a 2026 pressure-quench report and distinguishes an onset from zero resistance. Its new quantitative claims have not received a primary-text check in this pilot and are not included as verified comparison records. Metastable pressure-treated material must remain distinct from an equilibrium ambient-pressure phase. The omission and review limitation are preserved in the editorial mapping.

## Discovery implications

A useful mechanism predicts more than a plausible energy scale: it should connect an interaction model to gap symmetry, a material trend and a falsifiable observation. Spin-fluctuation, RVB and lattice-related approaches have different assumptions and outstanding tests. Treat their coexistence in a review as competing explanations, not a combined proof. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

## Related topics

See [magnetic evidence](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [spin-liquid and RVB proposals](/scwiki/spin-liquids-and-superconductivity), and [Planckian transport](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation).

articles.body:
## Scope

Iron-based superconductors include Fe-pnictogen and Fe-chalcogen layers in several structural families. Their low-energy electronic structure commonly involves several Fe 3d orbitals. Many parent compounds are metallic with coupled magnetic, structural or nematic order; this is a different starting point from a simple single-band cuprate analogy. Kamihara and colleagues' F-doped 1111 material established the early high-temperature platform. [R1](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7)

Distinguish 1111, 122, 111 and 11 materials, and treat a single-layer interface separately from a bulk crystal. The K-doped 122 superconductor reported by Rotter and colleagues is not the undoped BaFe2As2 parent. The discovery of superconductivity in FeSe likewise does not imply that its excess-Fe content or electronic structure can be ignored. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e) [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322)

## Mathematical assumptions

A multiband description uses gaps $\Delta_i(\mathbf k)$ on a measured set of bands or orbitals. A candidate s± solution has a relative sign between appropriate Fermi-surface sheets. It is a pairing-model result, not a consequence of the material containing iron. Changes in Fermi surfaces, shallow bands or orbital weights can change which candidate is favored. [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

Doping notation also needs care. The numerical coefficient $x$ in $\mathrm{BaFe}_{2-x}\mathrm{Co}_x\mathrm{As}_2$ differs from the fraction $x$ in $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x}\mathrm{Co}_x)_2\mathrm{As}_2$. Comparing “optimal x” values without converting their definitions can manufacture a disagreement. This pilot avoids a universal optimum or a universal orbital-coupling table.

## Experimental criteria

Report structural family, composition, sample form, preparation and pressure with each superconducting observation. Separate a parent magnetic or structural transition from a superconducting transition in a substituted compound. State whether a temperature is an onset, zero resistance, bulk response or spectroscopic gap scale. Unknown criteria remain unknown in the structured records.

The Fe1.01Se pressure result is a concrete condition check: the cited report associates 36.7 K with 8.9 GPa, not an unqualified 1-2 GPa result. That value cannot be copied into an ambient-pressure materials entry. Formula and pressure accompany it in the HTML and API record. [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b)

## Evidence for gap structure

The superconductivity-induced neutron response of Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2 constrains sign-changing pairing models. It does not directly determine the gaps of all 1111, 122, FeSe or interface systems. A synthesis should state the measured wave vector, normal-state spectrum and candidate coherence-factor interpretation. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

For an interface, replica bands or a high ARPES gap-closing scale must retain their spectroscopic labels. A reconstructed single-layer Fermi surface may differ substantially from the canonical hole-electron-pocket model. This is why the interface article and the multiband article are separate from a bulk-family temperature comparison. [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Limits and disputes

Several orbitals and strong correlations provide useful organizing language, but they do not establish a universal pairing mechanism. Hund-related mass renormalization is not automatically a larger pairing eigenvalue. FeSe, strongly doped endpoints and interface systems are especially important tests of simple family-wide statements. A strong evidence chain for a candidate gap is different from a unique microscopic verdict. [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Discovery implications

Use controlled changes in structure, composition, strain and disorder to test a specific model. Preserve the distinction between modifying a Fermi surface and identifying the boson that pairs electrons. The most useful database entry is a condition-rich measurement linked to its original compound, not one universal iron-based critical temperature. [R1](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7) [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322) [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b)

## Related topics

Read [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [two-dimensional interfaces](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces).

articles.body:
## Scope

“Nickelate superconductivity” includes distinct structural and preparation routes. Infinite-layer RNiO2 films and bilayer Ruddlesden-Popper La3Ni2O7 crystals differ in layer geometry, oxygen coordination and electronic structure. Their temperatures should not be presented as continuous optimization of one material. Li and colleagues' 2019 discovery and Sun and colleagues' 2023 high-pressure report establish different experimental settings. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

The infinite-layer route uses epitaxial precursors and topotactic reduction. Oxygen stoichiometry, residual apical oxygen, reduction uniformity and the substrate can all matter. A nominal chemical formula does not prove identical electronic states across bulk powders, supported films and membranes. This pilot does not infer a universal exchange energy or a common one-band model from the resemblance of NiO2 and CuO2 planes. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

## Mathematical assumptions

An orbital label such as $d_{x^2-y^2}$ or $d_{z^2}$ identifies part of a model basis; it does not by itself identify the pairing channel. A proposed gap or coupling matrix needs a declared band structure, filling, interaction and structural phase. Similar local configurations can motivate a cuprate analogy, but do not transfer a phase diagram or a numerical pairing scale to nickelates. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

Pressure changes can involve structural rearrangement as well as electronic bandwidth. For a bilayer crystal, a model evaluated in one structural phase must be compared with measurements in the same pressure regime. Distinguish calculations suggesting a favorable orbital configuration from observations establishing superconducting signatures. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Experimental criteria

Record family, layer count, rare-earth composition, sample form, reduction procedure, oxygen content and substrate. Keep resistance onset, zero resistance, magnetic response and superconducting fraction separate. If a field-induced or re-entrant state is proposed, include field direction and the temperature of the measurement rather than substituting a characteristic field for an upper critical field.

The Li source reports a transition range around 9–15 K in infinite-layer films; its individual criteria remain unextracted here. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

Sun2023 reports a resistance onset of 80 K at 18.5 GPa in run 1 without pressure medium. Run 2 uses KBr and shows an onset of 78 K at 18.9 GPa. The 77 K magnetic response is a separate measurement at 25.2 GPa. Residual resistance is explicitly discussed in the methods; these records must not be relabeled as zero resistance. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Limits and disputes

An 80 K high-pressure bilayer observation is not ambient-pressure bulk superconductivity. Likewise, a strained film and a pressure-treated crystal need not follow an identical structural path. The 2026 film, membrane, oxygen-cycling and magnetic-substitution updates in the pinned chapter require separate primary-text checks. This pilot retains their review debt rather than adding their numbers to a quantitative record. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853) [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9)

The pairing symmetry and microscopic interaction remain inference questions. A theoretical s± candidate, an orbital-selective interpretation or a magnetic compensation scenario must keep its theoretical or hypothetical label until supported by the corresponding phase-sensitive or field-resolved evidence. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Discovery implications

Compare controlled sample series within a structural family before making cross-family claims. A useful design experiment separates oxygen, strain, interface and carrier changes as far as possible. Negative controls are especially valuable when two substrates both produce compression but only one preparation yields a transition. Such observations constrain a mechanism without proving that one structural variable is sufficient. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9)

## Related topics

Read [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), [two-dimensional interfaces](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces), and [strain tuning](/scwiki/strain).
